nearest_works.work: Ganzeboom, De Graaf & Treiman, "A Standard International Socio-Economic Index of Occupational Status" (ISEI)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: A new continuous measure of socioeconomic position, scored for 271 detailed ISCO occupation units, that outperforms the existing alternatives (SIOPS prestige, EGP class) as a general-purpose stratification variable.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Construction on 73,901 men, 31 datasets, 16 countries. Convergent validity: r=.76 with SIOPS prestige, r=.90 with ISEI-scaled EGP10. Criterion validity across FOUR relationships in a standard status-attainment model, with the two relationships used in the optimisation reported separately from the two that were not, precisely so overfitting could be judged. OUT-OF-SAMPLE validation on five fresh datasets never used in construction (US OCG-1962, Australia 1973, Brazil, and two others). Head-to-head nested F-tests against EGP (Models A/B/C/D): A = EGP dummies alone; B = EGP + ISEI, testing whether EGP is internally homogeneous w.r.t. the criterion; C = ISEI alone, testing whether nine degrees of freedom buy anything; D = a parsimonious additive version with self-employment and supervisory status entered separately — i.e. an explicit test that the new measure is not just the old scheme's components recombined. Attenuation coefficients for collapsed versions so others can correct for aggregation. Closes by publishing the full scores and inviting the field to use them.

nearest_works.work: Weeden & Grusky, "The Case for a New Class Map" (microclasses)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: That the conventional big-class maps (EGP, Featherman–Hauser) and the gradational scales are the wrong unit, and that detailed occupations are the real site of class formation.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 55 individual-level outcome variables spanning FOUR topical domains (life chances; lifestyles/consumption/institutional participation; culture/political attitudes; demographic composition), from GSS 1972–2002 plus CPS. Log-multiplicative association models decomposing the occupation-by-outcome association into between-big-class and within-class components, run against EGP, Featherman–Hauser, AND an SES gradational scale. Classical significance tests (disaggregate models favoured on 49–51 of 55 outcomes) plus BIC, with the BIC disagreement reported rather than buried. A resampling exercise drawing GSS-sized samples from CPS to prove residual within-class association was not parameterised noise. Full per-outcome results in appendix tables B1–B3. Their explicit methodological argument is the one that bites here: validating a class map against "a criterion variable that has been nominated, seemingly by fiat, as especially important" is "no longer defensible" for an omnibus measure of social position, and Evans's few-preferred-criteria approach "does not provide the comprehensive assessment that an omnibus measure of life conditions demands."

nearest_works.work: Evans, "Testing the Validity of the Goldthorpe Class Schema" (with Evans & Mills, "Latent Class Analysis of the Criterion-Related and Construct Validity of the Goldthorpe Class Schema")
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: That EGP's employee classes are criterion-valid — that the categories track the occupational characteristics the theory says define them.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: A British national probability survey with a criterion set chosen FROM THE THEORY, not from convenience: employment and payment conditions, future prospects, control over work activities, authority relations, pay levels. Evidence reported at two tiers — the characteristics central to the concept (service relationship vs labour contract) and the secondary distinguishing characteristics — and the pattern of relative association strengths across the two tiers used as the test, not just the sign. The 1998 companion added latent class analysis of the schema's INTERNAL STRUCTURE, i.e. whether the postulated category structure is the one the data support. Even this — a purpose-built, theory-derived criterion battery — was later judged too narrow by Weeden & Grusky.

nearest_works.work: Oesch, "Coming to Grips with a Changing Class Structure"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: A new class schema adding a HORIZONTAL axis (work logic: technical / organisational / interpersonal, plus a fourth INDEPENDENT work logic separating employers and the self-employed from wage-earners) to the vertical skill axis. This is the closest published analogue to S10's off-hierarchy FREE level.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Four countries (Britain/BHPS, Germany, Sweden/LNU 2000, Switzerland), each with its own national occupational classification at 3-digit detail (216–298 codes). FOUR criterion outcomes chosen to test the two axes separately: earnings and promotion prospects to validate the vertical dimension; party support and union membership to validate the horizontal one — i.e. each axis had to earn its own evidence, and the horizontal axis was validated on outcomes the vertical axis does not predict. Results reported per country ("in all four countries, routine service workers come last"). Explicitly flags that assigning occupations to work logics "provides large ground for disagreement." Publishes the complete ISCO-88 code-to-class crosswalk as an appendix so the schema is transportable.

nearest_works.work: Chan & Goldthorpe, "Is There a Status Order in Contemporary British Society? Evidence from the Occupational Structure of Friendship" (with the ASR companion, "Class and Status: The Conceptual Distinction and its Empirical Relevance")
nearest_works.venue_year: European Sociological Review 20(5):383–401, 2004; and American Sociological Review 72(4):512–532, 2007
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: A new occupational STATUS scale, derived from association patterns rather than from attributes, and — the load-bearing claim — that status is empirically separable from class rather than a redundant relabelling of it.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Derivation from the occupational structure of close friendship via association models on a large national survey. Then a discriminant-validity programme: showed the recovered dimension is distinct from income, from education, and from socioeconomic status formed by income and education combined; showed it is gender-neutral; showed continuity with independently documented nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century status orders (an external, historical anchor); showed that some classes are status-homogeneous and others are not, which is what the Weberian claim requires. The 2007 ASR companion then ran class and status TOGETHER across several distinct outcome domains to demonstrate separable net effects in both directions — not merely that one absorbs the other.

nearest_works.work: Newlands & Lutz, "Occupational prestige and occupational social value in the United Kingdom: New indices for the modern British economy"
nearest_works.venue_year: Research in Social Stratification and Mobility 91:100935, 2024
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Two new rater-derived occupational indices, with the central claim that occupational prestige and occupational social value are "correlated but distinct" — structurally identical to S10's claim that altitude is distinct from EGP.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 2,429 respondents recruited via Prolific's UK-representative option (quota-matched on age, sex, ethnicity). Two SEPARATE rater samples (1,219 for prestige, 1,210 for social value) deliberately not overlapping, so the two constructs could not be primed by each other and would be statistically independent — the discriminant claim was designed into the data collection, not asserted afterwards. 576 occupation titles aligned to ISCO-08, with a 130-title core list, one per ISCO-08 minor group, so the indices are joinable to any ISCO-coded dataset. Documented data-quality screening (response-time and straightlining exclusions with matched replacement). Face-validity reported through the extremes (highly educated occupations top, stigmatised and illicit occupations bottom).

nearest_works.work: Smith & Son, "Measuring Occupational Prestige on the 2012 General Social Survey"
nearest_works.venue_year: GSS Methodological Report No. 122, NORC, October 2014 (fourth in the NORC series: North-Hatt 1947, Hodge–Siegel–Rossi 1963–65, GSS 1989)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Updated population-derived prestige scores for the full US occupational classification. The direct precedent for anything called a "folk ladder."
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 1,001 human raters drawn from the 2008 GSS reinterview panel — a probability sample of US adults, not a convenience pool. 860 occupational titles rated, 20 administered to every respondent as a common anchor and 840 rotated across 12 sub-samples. The instrument is literally a nine-box ladder with box 1 labelled BOTTOM, box 5 MIDDLE and box 9 TOP — S10's folk ladder is a four-level version of this exact object, which makes the comparison unavoidable. Item-specific non-response reported per occupation (0.0%–23.7%, with the worst-performing titles named). Procedure held identical to 1989 and 1963–65 so the new scores are comparable to the old series, and mapped onto every code in the 2010 SOC so the result is a usable instrument rather than a study-specific index.

field_standard: [BOTH TIERS] A construction rule stated fully enough that an independent team could rebuild the measure from the published description alone — element list, weights, signs, and every scale-resolution decision. Oesch, Ganzeboom et al., Smith & Son and Newlands & Lutz all publish this; it is the entry fee, not a virtue.
[BOTH TIERS] Reported inter-coder reliability for the occupational CODING step (assigning a person to an occupation code), separate from any reliability of the scale itself.

[BOTH TIERS] Face validity through the extremes: the occupations the measure ranks highest and lowest, shown, so a reader can judge whether the construct is the one named. Newlands & Lutz report exactly this.
[BOTH TIERS] At least one criterion association, with covariates, robust to reasonable specification changes.

[BOTH TIERS] A head-to-head joint model against the field-standard alternative (EGP or ISEI), reported in BOTH directions — does the new measure absorb the old, and does the old absorb the new. Ganzeboom's Models A/B/C/D is the canonical form.

[BOTH TIERS] An explicit statement of who the measure misclassifies and why. Hauser & Warren (Sociological Methodology, 1997) is the standing warning: they dismantled the composite SEI by showing it weights occupational earnings too heavily and misfits occupations held predominantly by women, and recommended using the components separately. Any new composite is now expected to pre-empt that decomposition.

[BOTH TIERS] If the measure is built on O*NET, engagement with Handel, "The O*NET content model: strengths and limitations" (Journal for Labour Market Research 49(2):157–176, 2016): item wording and response options are often vague, and there are gaps and duplication in content — so element-level results need to survive the removal of the vaguest items.

[NEW MEASURE ONLY] RELIABILITY, in a named form with a number. For a composite: internal consistency across its elements. For anything rater-derived: inter-rater reliability (ICC) with the rater population described. For a resampled construction: split-half reliability of the scores when the measure is rebuilt from disjoint halves of the coding passes. None of the six comparator works skipped this; it is the single most reliable thing a social-measurement referee checks first.
[NEW MEASURE ONLY] CONVERGENT VALIDITY against at least two established measures, correlations reported. ISEI reported r=.76 with SIOPS and r=.90 with scaled EGP10 before claiming anything.

[NEW MEASURE ONLY] DISCRIMINANT VALIDITY against the nearest existing construct, designed in rather than asserted. Chan & Goldthorpe showed status distinct from income, education AND combined SEI; Newlands & Lutz used two non-overlapping rater samples so their two indices could not contaminate each other. "It absorbs the old measure in a joint model" is one half of this test, not the whole of it.

[NEW MEASURE ONLY] CRITERION VALIDITY ON MULTIPLE OUTCOMES SPANNING MORE THAN ONE DOMAIN. Weeden & Grusky: 55 outcomes, four domains. Oesch: four outcomes, deliberately split so each axis of the schema was validated on outcomes the other axis does not predict. Evans: five theory-derived occupational characteristics at two tiers. This is the item on which S10 is furthest from the field, and Weeden & Grusky wrote the objection in advance: validating a social-position measure against "a criterion variable that has been nominated, seemingly by fiat, as especially important" is not defensible for an omnibus measure.

[NEW MEASURE ONLY] OUT-OF-SAMPLE VALIDATION ON DATA NOT USED IN CONSTRUCTION. ISEI: five fresh datasets, with the relationships used in the optimisation reported separately from those that were not. Weeden & Grusky: two independent surveys. Oesch: four national surveys.

[NEW MEASURE ONLY] INTERNAL-STRUCTURE EVIDENCE that the postulated category structure is the one the data support, not merely one the data tolerate. Evans & Mills (ESR 1998) used latent class analysis on EGP for exactly this. In the AERA/APA/NCME Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (2014) this is one of the five named sources of validity evidence — content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables, consequences — and a measurement referee will name that framework.

[NEW MEASURE ONLY] TRANSPORTABLE SCORING: a complete, published crosswalk from a standard occupational classification to the measure, covering the whole classification and not just the occupations that happened to appear. Ganzeboom scored all 271 ISCO units; Smith & Son covered every 2010 SOC code; Oesch appended the full ISCO-88 mapping; Newlands & Lutz aligned 576 titles to ISCO-08 with a 130-title core. A measure others cannot join to their own data is an index, not a measure — and every one of these authors closes by inviting the field to use the instrument rather than by arguing its novelty.

[NEW MEASURE ONLY] CROSS-POPULATION COMPARABILITY when the measure is applied across countries — evidence that the measure MEANS the same thing in each population, not merely that its effect has the same sign. Treiman's Occupational Prestige in Comparative Perspective (1977) established the genre by reporting the cross-national correlations among ~55–60 national prestige scales; the modern form is a measurement-invariance or alignment test, with partial invariance reported honestly where full invariance fails.

[NEW MEASURE ONLY] A stated rater population when the measure claims to capture a POPULAR or folk concept. NORC used 1,001 adults from a probability panel; Newlands & Lutz used a UK-representative quota sample. "Folk" is a claim about a population, and the field reads it as one.
we_meet: Construction rule published in full — every element id, name, level, sign and coder count in Appendix C, plus the scale-family resolution, the 3.A.1 collapse, and a committed --drop-3a1 sensitivity run (§3.4). This meets or exceeds what Oesch, Ganzeboom et al. and Smith & Son published.

Inter-coder reliability for the occupational coding step: two independent blind Claude passes over a shared rubric, 96.4% raw agreement, disagreements adjudicated, record committed as provinces/occupation_coding.json. This is the one reliability number the field asks for that S10 already has.

Head-to-head joint model against the field-standard alternative, in the ISEI Models A/B/C/D form: EGP's class block falls to p=0.56 beside the altitude ladders, and §4.6b reports the reverse direction too (each block strong alone; the folk ladder the stronger carrier, p=0.0008 with both in).

Blind construction — the coders were never shown the register, the hypothesis, or any outcome (§3.4). None of the six comparator works had this property; Oesch explicitly named schema-assignment judgement as the weak point of his own construction and could offer no remedy.

Preregistration of a directional ordering (free < front-line < corporate) and of a specific non-obvious ordinal contrast (the apex delta, middle − top) before any element was joined to the register, with a minute-level timeline and commit hash f10d502. No comparator preregistered anything. This is genuinely ahead of the field.

A confirmed risky prediction: the apex delta came out +0.049 (t 3.3), +0.067 (t 3.9) under full covariates, in the registered direction. Earning credit on a pre-committed ordinal contrast is stronger evidence of construct meaning than any of the six works attempted.

Replication of the headline effect across 22 chambers with an inverse-variance meta (free level −0.070 per sd, z = −5.0; negative in 21 of 22) and era stability 1997–2026 — on effect-stability grounds this exceeds Oesch's four countries and Evans's single survey.

Two semi-independent constructions (folk and theoretical ladders) correlating +0.75 to +0.92, with a never-together rule and widened errors shown where both enter — a within-instrument triangulation analogous in spirit to ISEI's ISEI/SIOPS/EGP comparison, though not a substitute for it.

Failed registered predictions reported, not suppressed — the altitude quadratic is recorded as null in Appendix A. This is the consequences-and-misfit honesty the Hauser–Warren tradition demands, applied to the measure's own predictions.

gaps.gap: ONE CRITERION VARIABLE. The measure's only external association is the register it was built to explain. Weeden & Grusky wrote the referee report in 2005: validating a measure of social position against "a criterion variable that has been nominated, seemingly by fiat, as especially important" is "no longer defensible" for an omnibus measure — and they said that of Evans's five theory-derived criteria, which is five more than S10 has. Oesch validated each axis of his schema on outcomes the other axis does not predict; S10's FREE level and its apex delta are both validated on the same single variable, so nothing distinguishes "altitude measures social position" from "altitude predicts this register."
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Build a criterion battery of 4–6 outcomes in at least two domains from data already in analysis/s10/. Career attainment: ministerial-office attainment from office_share.json (does altitude predict reaching executive office, net of tenure and party?); tenure and re-election survival from the member panel; committee or front-bench role if codable from the existing bios. Visibility: the Wikipedia prominence measure already used as a covariate in §4.7, entered as an outcome instead. Speech behaviour independent of the register: contributions per sitting, mean contribution length, genre mix (scripted vs unscripted share, which the study already partitions). Report the ladder's association with each, with the free level and apex delta broken out, in a single table — the Oesch layout, four to six columns.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable from data S10 already holds. office_share.json, the prominence measure and the contribution counts all exist; this is a join and a table, not new collection. Do NOT count the Pangram detector rate as a second criterion — it is a second instrument for the same construct, so it buys convergence, not criterion breadth, and should be labelled as such.

gaps.gap: NO RELIABILITY OF ANY KIND FOR THE LADDER ITSELF, and the 18 "blind coders" are not 18 independent coders. They are 18 sampled passes from one model family over one rubric — correlated draws whose effective independent N is unknown and probably small. A consensus threshold of "nominated by more than one coder" over 18 correlated draws is a much weaker filter than it reads as. Every comparator reported reliability in some form; a social-measurement referee checks this before anything else.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Three analyses, all re-runs of existing artifacts. (1) Split-half reliability: partition the 18 passes into disjoint halves, rebuild the consensus signature and the per-occupation level scores from each half independently, correlate the two score vectors per level, report Spearman–Brown corrected. (2) Coder-resampling curve: rebuild from k = 2, 4, 8, 12, 18 passes and plot score stability against k, which shows directly whether 18 was enough or whether the effective N saturated at 4. (3) Cross-model agreement: re-run workflows/element_levels.js nomination with at least two non-Claude models and report element-level agreement and the correlation of the resulting per-occupation scores with the current ones. Then refit the headline free-level and apex-delta results on each alternative signature.
gaps.feasibility: (1) and (2) are pure re-analysis of element_levels.json — hours, no new data. (3) needs API calls to other model families over the same 295-element rubric; cheap, and S10 already runs multi-model infrastructure for the log-prob work.

gaps.gap: THE WORD "FOLK" IS DOING WORK THE EVIDENCE DOES NOT SUPPORT. "Folk ladder" names a claim about how ordinary people picture a corporate hierarchy, evidenced entirely by an LLM's rendering of that stereotype. The precedent is unusually exact and unusually unforgiving: NORC's ladder is literally a nine-box column labelled BOTTOM / MIDDLE / TOP rated by 1,001 adults from a probability panel; Newlands & Lutz used 2,429 UK-representative raters. A referee reading "folk" will look for the rater population and find a model. Whose folk image, from which country's corporate vocabulary, is unanswered — and the five countries differ.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Either (a) rename — "model-elicited element weighting", "stereotype-composed ladder", or similar — and drop every sentence that implies a population holds this image, which costs nothing and removes the objection entirely; or (b) earn the word: recruit 200–400 quota-matched raters (Prolific, split across at least the UK and Canada given the chamber mix), have them do the same four-way nomination task on a stratified sample of the 295 elements or rate a sample of occupations directly onto the four levels, report ICC across raters, correlate the human consensus with the model consensus, and refit the headline results on the human-derived signature.
gaps.feasibility: (a) is a text edit and is the honest low-cost move. (b) is genuinely new collection — roughly the Newlands & Lutz design at a fifth of the scale, a few hundred pounds on Prolific and an ethics check. Note that (b) would also convert the model-vs-human correlation into a finding in its own right, which is the kind of result this study is otherwise good at.

gaps.gap: NO CONVERGENT VALIDITY AGAINST ANY ESTABLISHED OCCUPATIONAL MEASURE. ISEI reported r=.76 against SIOPS and r=.90 against scaled EGP10 before making any claim. S10 reports correlations only between its own two ladders (0.75–0.92), which establishes that two constructions of the same idea agree, not that the idea measures socioeconomic position. Until the ladder is placed against ISEI, SIOPS/prestige, occupational median wage and occupational mean education, "a measure of socioeconomic position" is an assertion.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Join the O*NET-SOC codes already assigned to each member to: ISEI and SIOPS via the published ISCO–SOC crosswalks; BLS OES median annual wage by SOC; O*NET Job Zone and required education by SOC; and the EGP class already coded. Report the full correlation matrix of the four altitude levels (and the apex delta) against all of these. Expect and report that TOP correlates strongly with wage and education — the informative numbers are what FREE does, and whether the four levels are separable in that matrix or collapse onto one wage-education dimension.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now. Every input is public (BLS OES, O*NET, ISCO-SOC crosswalks) and the SOC codes are already assigned. One afternoon.

gaps.gap: NO TRANSPORTABLE SCORING. The measure is scored for the occupations that happened to appear in 22 legislatures. Ganzeboom scored all 271 ISCO units; Smith & Son covered every 2010 SOC code; Oesch appended the full ISCO-88 crosswalk; Newlands & Lutz aligned 576 ISCO-08 titles. This is what separates a measure from an index in practice — and it is the cheapest item on this list.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Score all ~900 O*NET-SOC codes on the four levels (the element values exist for every SOC; nothing is legislature-specific about the scoring step) and publish the table as a CSV in analysis/s10/ and as an appendix, with the free/bottom/middle/top scores and an ISCO-08 crosswalk column. Include the standard error or coder-count-derived uncertainty per score.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now — level_scores.py already does exactly this computation on a subset. Running it over the full O*NET-SOC universe is a change of input scope, not a new method.

gaps.gap: THE FREE LEVEL — the study's distinctive axis and the source of its headline result — has no discriminant validity against the constructs it most resembles. EGP already has IVab (petty bourgeoisie / self-employed) and Oesch already has an "independent work logic" separating employers and the self-employed from wage-earners. A referee's first hypothesis will be that FREE is a self-employment dummy under a new name, and the joint-model absorption of EGP does not rule that out, because absorbing a seven-category class block is compatible with reproducing one of its categories.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Enter a binary self-employed / own-account indicator (derivable from the existing EGP coding, IVab plus IVc) alongside the free level in the register model and show the free level survives with its coefficient substantially intact. Then the sharper version: split FREE into its self-employed and its salaried-but-off-hierarchy members (a barrister in chambers versus an in-house counsel; an academic versus a corporate researcher) and show the effect is present in both halves. If it lives only in the self-employed half, the construct is Oesch's independent work logic and should be credited as such.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now — the EGP coding is committed (class_origin.py operates on it) and the FREE occupation list is small enough to split by hand.

gaps.gap: IS ALTITUDE JUST OCCUPATIONAL EDUCATION AND OCCUPATIONAL EARNINGS RECOMBINED? This is the Hauser & Warren (Sociological Methodology 1997) attack that ended the composite SEI's run: they decomposed it, showed it over-weighted occupational earnings and misfit women's occupations, and recommended using the components separately. Any new composite built from occupational attributes is now expected to pre-empt that decomposition rather than wait for it.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Regress each altitude level score on occupational mean education and occupational median wage (BLS OES, by SOC) and report R². Then enter the two components DIRECTLY in the register model alongside the ladder and show the apex delta and free-level effects survive. Separately, report which occupations the ladder places worst — specifically the caring, teaching and clerical occupations that sit awkwardly on any hierarchy axis and that are also the ones Hauser & Warren showed break composite indexes, and the ones most gender-skewed in the member population.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now from public BLS/O*NET data plus the existing member panel.

gaps.gap: NO INTERNAL-STRUCTURE EVIDENCE THAT THERE ARE FOUR LEVELS. The four-level structure is asserted from the folk image and the accountability theory, never tested against the data. Evans & Mills used latent class analysis on EGP for exactly this question; "internal structure" is one of the five named sources of validity evidence in the AERA/APA/NCME Standards (2014), and a measurement referee will name that framework by title. As it stands a reader cannot tell whether altitude is four things, two (on/off hierarchy, and height), or one.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Factor-analyse the occupation × 85-element matrix (and the 71-element theoretical version) and report whether a four-factor solution aligned with the assigned levels fits better than one- and two-factor alternatives, with fit statistics. Report the loading of each element on its assigned level versus the others — the elements that load on the wrong level are the interesting ones. Additionally: is FREE ordinally below BOTTOM, or is it off the dimension entirely? The registered ordering treats it as lowest; the theory says it is off-hierarchy. These are different structures and the data can distinguish them.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now — the occupation × element matrix is the input to level_scores.py.

gaps.gap: EFFECT STABILITY IS NOT MEASUREMENT INVARIANCE. The 21-of-22-chambers meta shows the effect has the same sign everywhere; it does not show the measure means the same thing in Northern Ireland as in Alberta. O*NET is a US instrument, the SOC coding is US-anchored, and the folk image of a corporate hierarchy is not obviously constant across five countries. Treiman established this genre in 1977 by reporting the correlations among ~55–60 national prestige scales before claiming cross-national validity; the modern form is an invariance or alignment test with partial invariance reported honestly.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Two tests. (1) Measurement-side: re-run the element-nomination workflow with country-specific framing (UK, Canadian, Australian corporate vocabulary) and correlate the resulting per-occupation level scores across the country variants — if the folk ladder is country-invariant, these correlate near the 0.75–0.92 the two ladders already achieve. (2) Model-side: a country × level interaction test on the register model, plus per-country refits of the ladder correlated against each other. Report where invariance fails rather than pooling over it — S10's own §4.6b already models per-chamber heterogeneity, so the machinery exists.
gaps.feasibility: (2) is fully computable now. (1) needs re-running the nomination workflow with varied framing — same cost as the cross-model check above, and best done in the same pass.

gaps.gap: THE FREE LEVEL RESTS ON 11 ELEMENTS OF 85, THE THINNEST BASE OF THE FOUR, AND CARRIES THE HEADLINE RESULT. The confirmed prediction (free lowest), the per-chamber meta (z = −5.0), and the joint-model absorption of EGP all run through a level defined by eleven O*NET descriptors. Handel's critique of O*NET item wording (Journal for Labour Market Research 2016) makes the fragility concrete: if two of those eleven are the vague ones, the result moves.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Leave-one-element-out jackknife of the FREE score across all 11 elements, refitting the register model each time, reporting the range of the free-level coefficient and the meta z. Add a bootstrap over the element set. Name the elements whose removal moves the result most and state whether they are among the O*NET items Handel flags as vaguely worded.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now — 11 refits of an existing model.

gaps.gap: MISSINGNESS ON THE MEASURE IS LARGE (n falls from 4,762 to 3,631 for the folk ladder, about 24%) AND IS PLAUSIBLY CORRELATED WITH THE FREE LEVEL ITSELF. The members whose prior occupation cannot be coded are disproportionately those with irregular, portfolio or unstated careers — which is close to a description of free work. If FREE members are differentially missing, the level's estimated coefficient is conditioned on the subset of free workers whose occupation was legible enough to code, and the headline is an artifact risk, not merely underpowered.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Tabulate missingness by chamber, era, party, gender and EGP class. Model the probability of a codable occupation and check whether it varies with the covariates that predict FREE. Report the register mean of the uncoded members against each coded level — if the uncoded sit near FREE, say so. Then bound the result: an inverse-probability-weighted refit, plus the worst-case bound in which all uncoded members are assigned to FREE and to TOP in turn.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now from the existing member panel and cov_targets_missing9.json.

gaps.gap: NO OUT-OF-SAMPLE VALIDATION. Every comparator validated on data not used in construction — ISEI on five fresh datasets, Weeden & Grusky on two independent surveys, Oesch on four national surveys. All of S10's evidence comes from one corpus and one criterion. Preregistration substitutes for this partially and genuinely, but it is a different guarantee: it rules out fitting the analysis to the result, not fitting the measure to the population.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: The strongest available version: hold out one country entirely, rebuild the consensus signature using only elements that survive nomination without reference to the held-out chambers, and refit. The cheaper version: chamber-level cross-validation of the free-level and apex-delta estimates. The genuinely external version: apply the published SOC-level scoring to any public survey carrying SOC-coded occupation plus an SES outcome (income, education, self-rated status) and show the ladder behaves as a socioeconomic measure outside legislatures at all — this is the single analysis that would most change how the measure reads.
gaps.feasibility: Held-out-country and chamber CV are computable now. The external-survey validation needs a public microdata acquisition (GSS, LFS, or Understanding Society) — modest new collection, and it depends on the transportable-scoring table above being built first.

gaps.gap: CONSTRUCTION CHOICES WERE MADE AFTER THE PREREGISTRATION, AND THERE ARE SEVERAL. The consensus threshold ("more than one coder"), the sign resolution, the scale-family resolution, the 3.A.1 collapse, the choice of 18 passes. The ordering was registered; the instrument was not frozen at the same moment. ISEI handled the analogous problem by explicitly separating the relationships used in the optimisation from those that were not, so a reader could see the overfitting risk directly.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: A specification curve over the construction grid — consensus threshold ∈ {2, 3, 4} coders; sign resolution variants; scale family variants; with and without 3.A.1; folk versus theoretical versus pooled — plotting the free-level coefficient and the apex delta across all cells with the preregistered specification marked. A stable band across the grid converts a defensible-choices footnote into evidence.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now — level_scores.py already parameterises most of these; this is a loop and a plot.

gaps.gap: NO KNOWN-GROUPS TABLE. A reader cannot currently see which occupations the ladder calls TOP and which it calls FREE. Newlands & Lutz report their hierarchy through its extremes precisely because it is the fastest way for a reader to check that the construct is the one named, and the cheapest way for an author to catch a sign error.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: A table of the ten highest- and ten lowest-scoring O*NET-SOC occupations on each of the four levels, with counts of legislators in each, plus the same for the apex delta. Include the occupations where the folk and theoretical ladders disagree most — those are the boundary cases that define what the measure is actually picking up.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable now; falls out of the transportable-scoring table.

surveys.verdict: S10 exceeds the field on three axes no comparator matched — preregistration of a directional ordering and a risky ordinal contrast before any element-outcome join, construction fully blind to the outcome, and effect replication across 22 chambers and three decades — but it is missing most of the classical construct-validation core (any reliability figure for the ladder, convergent correlations against ISEI/prestige/wage, discriminant separation of FREE from self-employment, criterion outcomes beyond the single variable the measure was built to explain, a transportable scoring table, and measurement invariance as distinct from effect stability), so as written it supports "a useful occupational index constructed for this study" but not "a new measure of socioeconomic position"; the good news is that eleven of the fourteen gaps are computable from artifacts already committed in analysis/s10/ plus public O*NET/BLS/ISEI crosswalks, and only two — human raters for anything called a "folk" ladder, and an external non-legislative dataset — require new collection.

nearest_works.work: Weixin Liang, Zachary Izzo, Yaohui Zhang, et al., "Monitoring AI-Modified Content at Scale: A Case Study on the Impact of ChatGPT on AI Conference Peer Reviews"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: 6.5%–16.9% of sentences in peer reviews submitted to ICLR 2024 / NeurIPS 2023 / CoRL 2023 / EMNLP 2023 could have been substantially LLM-modified (beyond spell-checking); corpus-level, not per-document.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: A maximum-likelihood distributional estimator over token frequencies (no per-document classification). Semi-synthetic validation at KNOWN ground-truth α ∈ {0, .05, .10, .15, .20, .25}: in-distribution error <1.8%, out-of-distribution (train on ICLR 2018–22, test NeurIPS'22 / CoRL'22) <1.8% / <2.4%. Pre-ChatGPT negative control returns α̂ ≈ 1.6%, inside the α=0 margin. Prompt-transfer test (train on one prompt, test on another) and model-transfer test (train GPT-3.5, detect GPT-4). A proofreading/light-edit experiment showing only a slight α̂ rise, far below the real-corpus effect. Head-to-head against instance-level baselines (3.4× lower in-dist error, 4.6× lower OOD). 95% CIs from 30,000 bootstrap samples. Part-of-speech sensitivity sweeps.

nearest_works.work: Weixin Liang, Yaohui Zhang, Mihai Codreanu, Jiayu Wang, Hancheng Cao, James Zou, "The Widespread Adoption of Large Language Model-Assisted Writing Across Society"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: By late 2024, ~18% of CFPB consumer-complaint text, up to 24% of corporate press-release text, ~10% of small-firm job-posting text, and ~14% of UN press-release text is LLM-assisted. The UN arm is the closest published analogue to institutional/official speech.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Same ICML estimator carried across four independent institutional corpora (687k complaints, 537k press releases, 304M postings, 15,919 UN releases), Jan-2022 → Sep-2024. Monthly time series with a pre-ChatGPT flat segment and an event-aligned inflection at Nov 2022 as the identifying evidence, plus a post-2024 plateau. Cross-domain replication of the same estimator is itself the robustness argument; subgroup breakdowns (firm age, firm size, state-level education) reported as covariate structure rather than as causal claims.

nearest_works.work: Dmitry Kobak, Rita González-Márquez, Emőke-Ágnes Horvát, Jan Lause, "Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: At least 13.5% of 2024 PubMed abstracts were LLM-processed; 5%–40% across subcorpora. Explicitly a lower bound.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 15.1M abstracts, 2010–2024. Counterfactual frequencies extrapolated from 2021–22 (2023 deliberately excluded as contaminated). Manual annotation of 900 excess words into style vs content; two INDEPENDENT marker sets built by different heuristics (291 rare style words, Δ=0.136; 10 hand-picked common words, Δ=0.134) whose near-identical answers serve as the internal replication. A historical placebo: 2013–2019 has no word with δ>0.01, and the COVID shock produced content nouns with Δ=0.069 — half the LLM effect and of a different lexical type. Explicit enumeration of why the number is a floor (abstracts using no marker word contribute nothing; sophisticated users strip marker words). No bootstrap CIs, no detector comparison, no human-labelled validation.

nearest_works.work: Lena Holzwarth, Rita González-Márquez, Dmitry Kobak, "Most biomedical publications show signs of LLM-assisted writing"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: 89% of 2025 open-access biomedical full texts show excess LLM-associated vocabulary; 68% in Discussion, 32% in Methods. Explicitly argues the earlier frequency-gap estimates (Kobak 13.5%, Gray) systematically UNDERSTATE prevalence.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: A new estimator β̂_LB = (q − p̂_human)/(1 − p̂_human) with p̂_human extrapolated from a 2018–2022 pre-period regression, maximised over a threshold grid. The headline validation is a SIMULATION with known ground truth: 100,000 documents/year, 500 simulated marker words, realistic parameter draws, recovering |β̂ − β| < 0.02 across the whole range β ∈ [0,1]. Delta-method standard errors with thresholds yielding SE ≥ 0.025 excluded. A section-length cropping control (255-word random windows) to show section differences are not a length artifact. Explicit mathematical argument for why the prior generation of estimators is biased downward. Notably absent: spike-ins, detector comparison, bootstrap CIs.

nearest_works.work: Minerva Suvanto, Andrea McGlinchey, Peter J. Barclay, Mattias Wahde, "Detecting undisclosed LLM-generated content in parliamentary texts"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Undisclosed LLM use in UK Commons written statements and Swedish Riksdag motions rises steadily from 2022: full-text detection rate 0.13% (2021) → 2.12% (2026) UK, 0.03% → 6.47% Sweden; paragraph-level 2.35% → 15.45% UK, 0.99% → 9.43% Sweden.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: A glass-box linear n-gram classifier (ICON) trained on 2014–2020 human text vs LLM regenerations of the same texts (Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite, GPT-5 mini) built from summaries, i.e. simulating the realistic office workflow rather than paraphrase. Held-out base-set FPR 6.2% (UK) / 4.3% (SWE). A FORWARD-SET false-positive anchor: the 2021 / 2021-22 slice of the same production corpus predates ChatGPT and yields exactly 1 false positive per language. A confidence-calibration histogram c(|s|) with an explicit FPR-vs-coverage operating curve across thresholds T=0…10 (their Figure 3), thresholds chosen at c ≥ 0.98. Two aggregation rules (whole-text vs any-paragraph) reported side by side. Length-threshold sensitivity (k = 10…60) and hyperparameter sweep. Interpretability offered as the answer to the false-accusation/bias objection.

nearest_works.work: Nathan Wolfrath, Simrin Patel, Madelyn Flitcroft, Anjishnu Banerjee, Melek Somai, Bradley H. Crotty, Anai N. Kothari, "Rising Prevalence of Detected AI-Generated Text in Medical Literature: Longitudinal Analysis in Open Access Articles"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: 2.7% of 7,251 JAMA Network Open articles (Jan 2022 – Mar 2025) contain significant AI-generated text; monthly share 0.0% (Jan 2022) → 11.3% (Mar 2025); highest in Invited Commentaries and Global Health.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: A single commercial detector (Originality.AI) at threshold 0.5 with a >10% AI-text document rule. Negative control = Jan-2022 articles, 0–2.2% flagged, acknowledged as error. Mann–Kendall monotonic trend test (p<0.001). A disclosure cross-check: of the 15 articles that disclosed LLM use, 40% were detected — declined as a recalibration basis for small n. NO second detector, NO confidence intervals, NO threshold sensitivity, NO recalibration. Limitations state detector variance and non-native-speaker bias. This is the nearest comparator in claim TYPE (commercial detector → institutional-corpus prevalence) and is markedly weaker than S10 on every calibration axis.

field_standard: A false-positive rate measured IN-DOMAIN on pre-2022 text drawn from the same corpus and same editorial pipeline — vendor benchmarks do not count (Liang: pre-ChatGPT ICLR α̂≈1.6%; Suvanto: pre-LLM slice of the production corpus; Wolfrath: Jan-2022 articles; Kobak: 2013–2019 placebo years).

An estimator-recovery experiment: semi-synthetic corpora built at KNOWN machine fractions α, pushed through the entire pipeline, reporting |α̂ − α| — in-distribution and out-of-distribution (Liang <1.8% / <2.4%; Holzwarth simulation |β̂−β|<0.02).

A generator-transfer check: the estimate must not depend on which model or which prompt produced the reference/synthetic machine text (Liang's prompt-transfer and GPT-3.5→GPT-4 transfer; Suvanto's two-model generation).

A human-edit / polish robustness result, in both directions: what a light copy-edit does to recall, and what a light machine polish of human text does to the false-positive rate (Liang's proofreading experiment; Saha et al. APT-Eval, ACL Findings 2025, where a commercial detector falls 92%→12% on lightly polished text and GLTR flags ~40% of minimal polishes).

A prevalence TIME SERIES whose pre-ChatGPT segment reads ≈0 and whose rise is event-aligned — not a single post-period level. Every one of the six comparators reports one (Kobak 2010–2024; Gray annual; Liang monthly; Suvanto annual per parliament; Wolfrath monthly).
An explicit direction-of-bias statement — lower bound, upper bound, or unbiased — with the argument (Kobak's lower-bound enumeration; Holzwarth's proof that the prior generation is biased downward).

Uncertainty quantification on the headline AND on every subgroup: bootstrap or delta-method intervals, clustered at the level the behaviour occurs (Liang's 30,000-sample bootstrap; Holzwarth's delta-method SEs).

A threshold/operating-curve sensitivity display: the estimate as a function of the decision threshold, shown against the FPR it buys (Suvanto's Figure 3, T=0…10; Liang's part-of-speech sweeps; Kobak's two independent marker sets).

A second, methodologically INDEPENDENT estimator run on the same corpus, with any disagreement adjudicated rather than narrated — the field's strongest evidence is agreement between a classifier and a distributional/word-frequency method that share no features.
A pinned, named, version-controlled instrument, with re-scoring stability reported — commercial detectors are moving targets (Jabarian & Imas, NBER WP 34223, 2025; the Epoch AI evaluation).

An estimand definition that separates drafting from polishing, translation, and grammar assistance, with the detector's behaviour on each named (Liang defines the estimand as 'substantially modified beyond spell-checking'; arXiv:2510.20810 argues detection accuracy falls monotonically with human revision and that bare accuracy numbers without stated prerequisites are uninterpretable).

A subgroup / differential-error audit against the attributes detectors are known to fail on — non-native English, seniority, register (Liang et al., Patterns 2023: 61.3% mean FPR across seven detectors on TOEFL essays vs ~0% on native-speaker controls; Wolfrath flags this as a stated limitation).
An adversarial-robustness statement, because a detection-based prevalence figure is only a floor if evasion is characterised (RAID, Dugan et al., ACL 2024).
Full reproducibility: scored data, code, sampling seeds, and the exact detector version attached to every verdict.
we_meet: In-domain pre-period specificity, at a grain no comparator reaches: 60 segments per chamber dated ≤2022-06-30 (not 2022-12-31), 1,260/1,260 Human, Wilson [99.7%, 100.0%], with each chamber's own editorial register checked separately. Suvanto anchors on one pre-LLM slice per parliament in two parliaments; Wolfrath on one month of one journal; Liang on semi-synthetic per-venue validation. S10's control design is the strongest in the set.

Explicit direction-of-bias with the arithmetic shown: Rogan–Gladen with Sp=1 measured and Se≤1 by construction gives τ = π/Se ≥ π, so the figure is a floor. This matches Kobak's lower-bound discipline and exceeds Wolfrath, who states no direction at all.

Bootstrap uncertainty on the headline (9.03% [8.00%, 10.08%]) and on all 20 chamber rates, using a cluster bootstrap over segments with a correct ratio-estimator framing — Wolfrath reports bare point estimates, Kobak reports no intervals.

Instrument version control, with a documented near-miss: the Pangram 3-vs-4 silent API default (11/20 agreement when unnamed, 20/20 when named), the 658-segment New Brunswick rescore (specificity identical 60/60, disagreements net upward — an undercount not a false-positive problem), and 360/360 agreement on the UK/Ireland rescore. No comparator reports vendor-version control.

A corpus-side distribution-shift audit performed BEFORE scoring: invisible-character contamination caught and stripped (Manitoba soft hyphens, 81.6% of segments vs 0.04% of 2006–19 tokens) and a transcription-regime diagnostic on words-per-sentence and contraction density that excluded Tasmania outright and floored NL/WAL/MB control windows. This is the corpus half of what critics of detector-based prevalence demand, and no comparator does it.

A frame-error audit that runs against the study's own interest: the Manitoba extractor was losing 42% of the record NON-randomly, precisely the prepared speeches where drafting concentrates (chamber reads 5.3% before repair, 13.1% after), and the controls are used as the check that this was a frame effect, not a detector effect.

Partial-document handling, which the entire comparator set lacks: 134 of 316 flagged segments are Mixed at mean fraction 0.435, and the study reports the fraction-weighted 9.03% rather than the naive AI+Mixed 12.03%, naming its own earlier figure as an error rather than a refinement.

Sampling-frame discipline: uniform draw over segments with a word-weighted ratio estimator, the length/drafting confound quantified (11.3% in the longest quartile vs 0.7% in the shortest), the ratio estimator's finite-sample bias checked (bootstrap 10.30% vs plug-in 10.31%), and the equal-weight chamber mean (9.12%) reported as a check that no large chamber drives the headline.

An adversarial bound making the floor claim empirical rather than rhetorical: directed evasion clears the detector on 11.1% of variants and 22.5% of targets (§4.9), with the honest scoping that this bounds the study's own effort, not an adversary's. No prevalence paper in the comparator set runs one.

A contemporary-specificity bound from a blind two-vote audit of all 316 flagged segments against the one stratum with near-certain human authorship (277 prepared / 21 unclear / 11 spontaneous on both votes), costing at most 0.17–0.38 points on the headline. This is a genuine answer to the transfer objection and goes beyond any comparator.

A second instance-level instrument reported in agreement (Opus screen, AUC 0.95) and two more (Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT) reported despite disagreeing — reporting a disagreeing instrument is above field practice.
Full reproducibility: per-number script footnotes, committed verdict CSVs with a version column, seeded sampling.

gaps.gap: The headline is fraction-weighted by an uncalibrated vendor output. 42% of flags are Mixed, their mean `fraction_ai` is 0.435, and this single continuous number carries the entire 12.03% → 9.03% correction — a 25% haircut on the claim. Nothing in the study, and nothing in the literature, shows that Pangram's `fraction_ai` tracks the true machine word share. If it is systematically low the headline is too low; if it is systematically high on human-dominant mixtures the headline is too high, and the floor argument does not protect a fraction-weighted estimator the way it protects a binary flag rate.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: A mixture-calibration experiment: build ~400 segments of KNOWN machine word fraction p ∈ {0.1, 0.2, …, 0.9} by splicing machine-drafted sentences into real pre-2022 chamber speeches at the sentence level (and at the paragraph level, since Mixed verdicts in the wild look like a drafted block inside spontaneous speech). Score them, regress reported `fraction_ai` on true p, report slope, intercept, residual SD, and behaviour at the extremes. Propagate the fitted calibration through `prevalence_report.py` and report the headline under raw, calibrated, and binary-AI-only weightings.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds. Splice source = the 1,260 pre-2022 control segments; machine source = the same generation pipeline that produced the 40-speech synthetic pilot. Cost is ~400 additional Pangram 4 calls and a fitting script. No new corpus collection.

gaps.gap: No end-to-end estimator-recovery at known α. This is the single most visible exhibit in the strongest comparators — Liang reports |α̂ − α| < 1.8% in-distribution and < 2.4% out-of-distribution across α ∈ {0, .05, …, .25}; Holzwarth reports |β̂ − β| < 0.02 across [0,1] by simulation. S10 validates its components (specificity 1,260/1,260; a 40-speech sensitivity pilot at 40/40, itself declared underpowered) but never validates the COMPOSED pipeline — segmenter → verdict → fraction weighting → word weighting → bootstrap — against a corpus whose true machine share is known. A referee reading `9.03%` will ask what the estimator returns when the answer is 9%.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Semi-synthetic recovery curve: for each of ~6 target values α ∈ {0, .025, .05, .10, .15, .20}, build a 300-segment pseudo-chamber by replacing α of the WORDS in real 2019 segments with machine-drafted speeches generated the way a legislative office would prompt (bill title, constituency, 2–3 talking points, chamber-appropriate length), run the full unmodified pipeline, and plot α̂ against α with bootstrap bands and the 45° line. Repeat once out-of-distribution — calibrate on one country's chambers, test on another — to mirror Liang's OOD arm.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds. Needs ~1,800 new Pangram calls and reuse of the existing generation and segmentation scripts. No new corpus collection. This is the highest-value single addition to the prevalence arm.

gaps.gap: No prevalence time series — and the 'current' window is not homogeneous, so the scalar 9.03% is a blend of a rising series whose value depends on the sample's date mix. In the committed verdicts the pooled segment flag rate is 145/1,428 = 10.15% in 2025 against 144/912 = 15.79% in 2026 (z ≈ 4.1). Every comparator reports a series with a flat pre-ChatGPT segment and an event-aligned rise; that series IS the evidence that a detector is measuring adoption rather than a level artifact. S10's series is a 0% pre-2022 control, a New-Brunswick-only ladder at 40–50 segments per year (2023: 1/50, 2024: 1/50), and a 2025–26 lump.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Three steps. (1) Free, today: report the headline and every chamber rate split by 2025 and 2026 with CIs, and state which estimand the 9.03% is. (2) Extend the year ladder to all 20 chambers at n ≈ 120 per chamber-year for 2023 and 2024, giving a five-point series 2022→2026 whose first two points are the existing 0%-controls. (3) Fit an interrupted time series on the DETECTOR arm with the break pre-set at ChatGPT's release, so it matches the register arm's ITS and the two instruments can be plotted on one axis.
gaps.feasibility: Step (1) is free from committed CSVs. Steps (2)–(3) are computable from data S10 already holds — the 2023–24 Hansard is already extracted; cost is ~2,400 additional Pangram calls. No new collection.

gaps.gap: The estimand says 'machine-drafted' but the instrument measures 'machine-touched'. Saha et al. (APT-Eval, ACL Findings 2025) show commercial detectors flag minimally polished human text — Originality.AI falls from 92% to 12% accuracy on lightly polished articles, GLTR misclassifies ~40% of extremely minor polishes as AI — and arXiv:2510.20810 argues detection accuracy declines monotonically with human revision, so a flag cannot separate 'a model wrote this' from 'a person wrote this and a model tidied it'. Liang guards this by defining the estimand as 'substantially modified beyond spell-checking' and running a proofreading control. S10 has no such control, so 'drafted' is the one word in the abstract the evidence does not license.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: A polish ladder run on text whose ideas and structure are entirely human: take ~200 pre-2022 control segments and pass them through graded machine polish (grammar-only; sentence-level rewrite; full stylistic rewrite preserving content), score each rung, and report the flag rate. If grammar-only polish flags, report a second number — 'machine-touched' alongside 'machine-drafted' — or narrow the abstract's wording. Pair with the converse ladder (machine draft → light copy-edit → member-voice rewrite → read-aloud-and-retranscribe, ~150 per rung) to get Se(rung) and the implied τ = π/Se band, which is what turns '9.03%' from a floor into an interval.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds. Source text is the existing controls; the bypass arm's (§4.9) generation scaffolding already does directed rewriting and can be re-pointed at non-adversarial polish. ~700 additional detector calls.

gaps.gap: The elevenfold cross-chamber spread is confounded with sample date-mix and genre-mix, neither of which is standardised. Per-chamber 2026 share of the current sample runs from 0.00 (SA, entirely 2025) to 0.57 (NL), while the pooled rate is 1.56× higher in 2026 than 2025 — so part of the spread is 'whose sample reaches further into 2026'. Genre is coded for CA-FED only (360 segments), yet §4.3 shows genre drives a large gradient, so chambers whose in-band record is more heavily scripted will read higher for reasons that are about business mix, not drafting propensity.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Direct standardisation: recompute every chamber rate on a common calendar window (or model date explicitly), and standardise to a common genre mix once genre is available panel-wide. Then a chamber × year logistic model with member random effects, reporting the between-chamber spread before and after adjustment. Report the raw 11× and the adjusted ratio side by side.
gaps.feasibility: The date half is free from committed CSVs today. The genre half is computable from data S10 already holds — it needs the LLM genre classifier the draft already scopes as future-work item 12, run over segment text the study has. No new collection.

gaps.gap: The spread is asserted rather than tested, and 'elevenfold' is a ratio of extremes over 20 noisy estimates, which is upward-biased by construction. No comparator reports a max/min ratio as its dispersion statistic. (The heterogeneity is real — a quick χ² on the committed prevalence verdicts gives 88.1 on 17 df across 18 chambers, I² ≈ 0.81 — which is exactly why the test is cheap to run and awkward to have omitted.)
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Fit a beta-binomial or logit-normal random-effects model across chambers; report the between-chamber SD τ, the heterogeneity test, and empirical-Bayes shrunken chamber rates. Quote the shrunken extreme ratio next to the raw 11× so the headline dispersion claim is a shrinkage-corrected quantity rather than an order statistic.
gaps.feasibility: Free. Computable from `pangram_p4_verdicts.csv` and `banded_prevalence.py` in roughly thirty lines. No new data of any kind.

gaps.gap: Prevalence intervals cluster on segments, not members. 2,340 prevalence segments come from 1,123 distinct speakers (2.08 each), and machine drafting is a member/office-level habit — one staffer's workflow produces many correlated flags. The draft already carries a flagged non-clustered-SE caveat in §4.6b and says the study 'has been bitten by this three times'; the prevalence arm has the same exposure and no caveat.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Re-run the ratio-estimator bootstrap resampling SPEAKERS within chamber rather than segments, and report the design effect. On the committed data the concentration is modest — 289 flags across 252 speakers, top-10 speakers carrying 9.3% of flags — so the intervals should widen slightly rather than break, which is the point: it costs nothing and removes a standing objection.
gaps.feasibility: Free. The `speaker` column is already in the committed verdict CSV.

gaps.gap: No independent estimator with a different error structure. The Opus screen (AUC 0.95) is an LLM judge keying on the same surface features as the detector — the study's own judge-leakage measurement (r = +0.758 between screen and grading-judge AI guesses) is the evidence that these are not independent instruments. The field's strongest triangulation is agreement between a classifier and a distributional/word-frequency estimator that share no features, and S10 already holds every input needed to build one.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Implement the Liang ICML-2024 maximum-likelihood distributional estimator on Hansard: reference human distribution = each chamber's pre-2022 record, reference machine distribution = the synthetic legislative speeches from the recovery experiment above, estimate α̂ per chamber-year from token frequencies alone, and plot α̂ against Pangram's word-weighted rate chamber by chamber. Two unrelated estimators landing on the same 9% converts a single-vendor number into a cross-validated one; a systematic offset is itself publishable and tells you which one is biased.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds — corpora, pre-2022 controls, open-model log-probs, and the synthetic generation pipeline are all in hand. No detector calls, no new collection. A few hundred lines.

gaps.gap: Two open detectors were run and DISAGREE, and the disagreement is narrated rather than adjudicated. `detector_trend_by_year.csv` shows Fast-DetectGPT flagging 6.2% in 2021 → 3.2% in 2025 → 2.4% in 2026 and Binoculars 4.8% → 3.0% → 1.9% — i.e. 2025–26 flag rates BELOW their own pre-LLM false-positive floors, and declining. The draft reads this as those detectors' sensitivity failure, which is plausible, but a referee sees one instrument saying 9% and two saying less than zero. The monotone DECLINE also needs an explanation, since it is the same direction the permeation finding predicts and could be read as the human baseline drifting into the detectors' machine-side score region.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Run Binoculars and Fast-DetectGPT on the SYNTHETIC legislative speeches from the recovery and edit ladders. If they miss known machine text at the rate they 'miss' it in the wild, the sensitivity-failure reading is demonstrated instead of asserted, and the disagreement becomes evidence for the floor rather than against it. Separately, score Pangram on the identical segment set the zero-shot detectors scored, so the three-way comparison is on the same text rather than on differently-drawn samples, and decompose the score decline into human-side drift versus machine-side drift.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds — the log-prob pipeline and the synthetic corpora exist; needs the shared segment set scored through Pangram (~600 calls).

gaps.gap: No differential-error audit against the attributes detectors are known to fail on. Liang et al. (Patterns 2023) — 61.3% mean FPR across seven detectors on TOEFL essays against ~0% on native-speaker controls — made this the field's reflex objection, and Wolfrath names it as a limitation. S10 holds exactly the covariates needed (birth year, seniority, prior occupation, class, education) and reports none of them against the flag rate, and never checks whether the 1,260 pre-2022 controls actually covered the members who generate the contemporary flags. A specificity of 1,260/1,260 pooled over members who are not the flagged members is a weaker guarantee than it looks.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Three cheap exhibits. (i) Flag rate by covariate cell in the current window, with the honest framing that an association is a finding about who uses the tools, not proof of detector bias. (ii) A control-coverage audit: what share of currently-flagged members have any pre-2022 control speech of their own, and how the control pool's covariate composition compares to the current speaker pool. (iii) For members present in both windows, a within-member specificity check — their own pre-2022 speech scored against their current flags.
gaps.feasibility: (i) and (ii) are free from data S10 already holds — verdict CSVs joined to the existing member covariate table. (iii) needs modest additional scoring of within-member pre-2022 text, still from held corpora.

gaps.gap: No threshold/operating-curve display. Suvanto's Figure 3 (FPR versus fraction-classified across T = 0…10) is the field's standard way of showing that a prevalence number is not a threshold artifact; Kobak's two independent marker sets and Liang's part-of-speech sweeps play the same role. S10 reports one operating point of one vendor's default decision rule, even though `fraction_ai` is a continuous column already in the committed data.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Sweep the headline as a function of a `fraction_ai` cut-off (and of a minimum-segment-length cut-off), plotting the estimated prevalence against the pre-2022 control flag rate that each cut-off buys. Show that the 9.03% sits on a plateau rather than on a cliff.
gaps.feasibility: Free. `fraction_ai` is in `pangram_p4_verdicts.csv`; the 1,260 controls supply the FPR axis.

gaps.gap: The pooled 9.03% has no stated population weighting. It is a uniform draw over segments pooled across chambers, cross-checked against an equal-weight chamber mean (9.12%). Neither is an estimate for 'the average word spoken in these legislatures', since chambers differ by more than an order of magnitude in words on the record. The two estimands answer different questions and the abstract does not say which one it is claiming.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Post-stratify to each chamber's actual in-band word volume and report the population-weighted rate alongside the chamber-average rate; name the estimand in the abstract ('the average chamber' versus 'the average word').
gaps.feasibility: Free. Per-chamber in-band word counts already exist in the extraction; `band_coverage_check.py` already computes the ingredients.

gaps.gap: No external corroboration of any kind for the cross-chamber spread. No comparator has ground truth either — Kobak's nearest move is comparing to self-report surveys (50–71%) — so this does not block. But 20 chambers is enough units for the first external validation anyone in this literature could run, and the spread is currently the study's least-defended headline claim ('what drives a chamber's position is not established here').
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: A per-chamber exposure measure to correlate against the flag rate: freedom-of-information / written-question requests on procurement of Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise or equivalent licences for members' offices and research services, plus the date each chamber issued AI guidance (a partial policy scan already exists in the study). Rank-correlate against chamber prevalence.
gaps.feasibility: NEW COLLECTION, but bounded and cheap — roughly 20 FOI/parliamentary-question filings against bodies that already answer them routinely, plus extension of the existing 22-chamber policy scan.

gaps.gap: Vendor-version drift is documented once, not monitored. §3.2 records a silent model-tier swap that changed 9 of 20 verdicts, which is the study's own proof that the instrument is a moving commercial target; a re-scoring stability panel is the natural follow-through and nobody in this literature does it.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Freeze a 300-segment panel spanning all chambers and both verdict classes, re-score it at a fixed interval, and report verdict and `fraction_ai` drift. Publish the distribution of the existing `version` column so every reported number is traceable to a specific model string.
gaps.feasibility: Cheap and computable from data S10 already holds — the panel is a subset of the committed verdicts; ~300 calls per repeat.

surveys.verdict: S10 exceeds the field standard on the axis it chose — 21 chambers of in-domain pre-period controls at 1,260/1,260 is the strongest specificity calibration in this literature, and its bias-direction discipline, corpus contamination audits, Mixed-fraction correction and evasion bound put it well above every detector-based prevalence comparator — but it falls short of the strongest population-level works on the three exhibits they are built on: an end-to-end recovery test at known machine fractions (Liang, Holzwarth), a prevalence time series with a flat pre-ChatGPT segment (all six comparators), and a validated mapping from the vendor's continuous Mixed fraction to actual machine word share, which is the uncalibrated step the 9.03% headline actually rests on.

nearest_works.work: Michel, Shen, Aiden, Veres, Gray, … Pinker, Nowak, Lieberman Aiden, "Quantitative Analysis of Culture Using Millions of Digitized Books" (culturomics)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Aggregate n-gram frequency series over 1800–2000 track real cultural and linguistic change (lexicon growth, grammatical regularisation, fame, censorship, collective memory).
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: ~5M books (~4% of all printed); yearly counts normalised by the year's total corpus size; a hand-curated English 1800–2000 subcorpus filtered on OCR and metadata quality (they explicitly discarded most scanned books for bad OCR/dates); external ground-truth validation for each claim (Nazi blacklists for the censorship series, Who's-Who for fame, dictionary sampling for lexicon size); per-word case series shown alongside every aggregate; full data release. Their weakness — no per-book metadata, so composition is unaudited — is what the next decade of critique was built on.

nearest_works.work: Pechenick, Danforth & Dodds, "Characterizing the Google Books Corpus: Strong Limits to Inferences of Socio-Cultural and Linguistic Evolution"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Most published diachronic-lexical trends from that corpus are artifacts of changing corpus composition, not of language or culture changing.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Showed the corpus is a library (one copy per book) not a readership sample, so one prolific author moves the series; showed the scientific-literature share grows steadily across the 20th century and reproduced several famous 'trends' as that composition shift; compared the 2009 and 2012 corpus versions and the fiction subcorpus to demonstrate version- and stratum-dependence of published results; reconstructed composition indirectly from marker vocabulary when metadata was withheld. Companion standard: Koplenig, DSH 32(1):169–188, 2017, reconstructing German corpus composition and showing 'censorship' effects dissolve into it.

nearest_works.work: Morin & Acerbi, "Birth of the cool: a two-centuries decline in emotional expression in Anglophone fiction"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: A word-list rate (emotion vocabulary) declined steadily across two centuries — the same statistical object S10 runs, over the same kind of window.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Replicated the series in two metadata-rich corpora alongside Google Books, so composition could be audited directly; ruled out author-age and author-gender demographic drift; ruled out vocabulary-richness change (the denominator problem); ruled out genre-prevalence change within the corpus; decomposed the aggregate into positive vs negative subsets and showed the effect lives in one subset only (i.e. per-word/subset decomposition, not a single pooled rate); tied the individual-level correlate (ageing) to the population-level trend. This is the closest published template for what a referee will want from S10.

nearest_works.work: Biber & Finegan, "Drift and the Evolution of English Style: A History of Three Genres"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: English written register drifted over four centuries along stable underlying dimensions — the canonical 'register moved over decades/centuries' claim.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Multi-feature dimensions (dozens of co-occurring surface features reduced to three interpretable dimensions from a prior synchronic factor analysis), not a single word list; genre held fixed by design — three genres tracked separately across the same periods, with the shared direction across genres carrying the argument; period sampling from matched, documented sampling frames (ARCHER-lineage); each genre's trajectory reported separately so no pooled line could hide a composition shift; interpretation checked against independent social history.

nearest_works.work: Mollin, "The Hansard hazard: gauging the accuracy of British parliamentary transcripts"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Hansard is not verbatim: editorial intervention systematically removes and rewrites exactly the stance/register features corpus studies key on, and editorial practice has changed over time.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Against-the-original validation — the same speeches compared to broadcast/audio, quantifying what editors delete (e.g. emphatic adjectives reduced by ~75%); an editorial survey of the Official Report's own staff and style rules; documentation that reporting is 'thrice removed' (live reporters in shifts → editing staff → next-morning compilation). This is the field's standard for any register claim built on an edited parliamentary record, and it establishes editorial-convention change as the default rival explanation.

nearest_works.work: Gries & Hilpert, "The identification of stages in diachronic data: variability-based neighbour clustering" (VNC)
nearest_works.venue_year: Corpora 3(1):59–81, 2008; extended in The Oxford Handbook of the History of English, OUP 2012, 134–144
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Onsets and periods in diachronic corpus series must be estimated bottom-up from the data, not read off a plotted minimum or imposed a priori.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: A clustering estimator over temporally adjacent bins with an explicit criterion for how many stages the data support; demonstration on multiple change series that eyeballed periodisations differ from data-driven ones; released implementation. The econometric sibling standard a quantitative referee will apply instead: Bai & Perron, Econometrica 66(1):47–78, 1998 and J. Applied Econometrics 18(1):1–22, 2003 — a test that a break exists against a no-break/smooth-trend null, a break date with a confidence interval from the estimator, and sensitivity to the number of breaks.

field_standard: Corpus composition is measured per time bin, not assumed: report the sampling frame, document counts and source identity per year, and re-run on a composition-stabilised panel (Pechenick 2015; Koplenig 2017).

Genre/text-type mix inside each time bin is either stratified or reweighted to a fixed composition, and the trend is shown to hold within at least one narrow genre present in every year (Biber & Finegan 1989; Morin & Acerbi's genre-prevalence control).

Text-production and transcription regime is documented per source and per period, with an against-the-original or documentary validation; editorial-convention change is treated as the default rival, not a footnote (Mollin 2007).

Digitisation provenance (born-digital vs OCR) is stated per source-year with a machine-readable quality proxy, and the trend is shown orthogonal to it (Michel 2011's curated subcorpus; Lansdall-Welfare et al., PNAS 114(4):E457–E465, 2017).

Aggregate word-list results are decomposed to the word level: per-word slopes, fraction moving, sign/rank test against the placebo pool's slope distribution, and a trimmed aggregate showing no small subset carries it (Morin & Acerbi's positive/negative split).
Dispersion is reported alongside frequency: the share of documents and of speakers moving, not only the pooled corpus rate (Egbert & Biber, Corpora 14(1):77–104, 2019; Gries on dispersion measures).

The word list is shown independent of the outcome it is used to demonstrate: placebo lists matched on pre-period trend as well as frequency, plus replication with a list derived from an unrelated corpus.

Inference accounts for token non-independence: bootstrap/permutation over documents and speakers, never chi-square or log-likelihood over pooled token counts (Lijffijt, Nevalainen, Säily, Papapetrou, Puolamäki & Mannila, DSH 31(2):374–397, 2016).

The normalisation denominator is justified and the result shown robust to it — per-million-words rate vs per-document presence vs proportion of a matched reference vocabulary (Baker, J. English Linguistics 39(1):65–88, 2011, on equal-sized matched sampling frames).

A dated onset requires a formal break test against a smooth-trend null, a break date with a CI produced by the estimator, and sensitivity to the assumed number of breaks (Gries & Hilpert 2008; Bai & Perron 1998/2003).
Population turnover is separated from within-individual change by panel/fixed-effects decomposition before a community-level drift is claimed (Sankoff & Blondeau, Language 83(3):560–588, 2007).

The standing named rival mechanism in the literature is confronted with its own instrument, not paraphrased — for late-20th-century public discourse that is informalization/conversationalization (Fairclough, Discourse and Social Change, Polity 1992; Pearce, Language and Literature 14(1):65–90, 2005, with 28 Longman-grammar markers over 1966–97).
The drift is replicated in at least one independent corpus with a different sampling frame (Morin & Acerbi's two metadata-rich corpora; Baker's four matched reference corpora).
Series are reproducible from raw counts, with code and per-word data released (Michel 2011; Kobak et al.'s public repository).
we_meet: Ruler fixed independently of the years measured — the marker set and 200 frequency-AND-dispersion-matched placebo sets are built once and applied unchanged to every chamber and every year (§4.5a, occurrence_trends.py). This is the single control most culturomics work lacks, and the reported statistic being an instrument-minus-placebo gap rather than a raw rate absorbs most of checklist item 9 (denominator robustness) and part of item 6 (dispersion enters the matching).

Composition stabilised across chambers when pooling, with the failure mode named explicitly — 'a pooled line whose membership changes between years is a picture of the download schedule, not a trend' (footnote r45a) — and constant-window endpoint tables (2006–2026, n=19; 1994–2026, n=3) rather than a ragged pooled series (§4.5a, constant_window_trend.py).

Transcription-regime diagnostic run per chamber-year on convention-tracking markers (words per sentence, contraction density), with Tasmania excluded outright for a 3.4→15.9/1,000 contraction step falling between windows, and NL/WAL/MB controls floored to their current regime (§2.1, transcript_regime_check.py). Partial coverage of checklist item 3, and more than most parliamentary-corpus work does.
A period-correlated contamination hazard found and removed rather than assumed absent — Manitoba soft hyphens in 81.6% of 2025–26 segments vs 0.04% of 2006–19 tokens, stripped at build time (§2.1).

In-time placebo: the Kobak estimator run on pre-LLM window pairs where the true effect is zero by construction, and it fires (§3.3, in_time_placebo.py). This is the actual evidence behind the 'blind to steady drift' half of the claim.
Regression-to-the-mean guard on the convergence result via disjoint baseline (2006–08 means) and growth (2010–2026) windows, ρ = −0.51 against −0.56 on the coupled version (§4.5a).
