Clustered resampling for the onset date — 2,000 bootstrap resamples of sitting days within year put the minimum at 1994 in 84.8%, 1995 in 13.0%, 1996 in 2.1% (footnote r45, long_trend_bootstrap.py). Correct family of inference per Lijffijt et al. 2016, applied to the date.

Per-chamber replication of the level effect against each chamber's own pre-2022 counterfactual, Fisher-combined over 47 confirmatory specifications with the discovery corpus (New Brunswick) held out and reported separately (§4.5b, cross_corpus.py).

A rival mechanism partly confronted with data: where a data-defined formality control exists (Ireland, CA-FED, UK), register excess exceeds the formality gap in every case (UK +0.26 vs +0.09) (§4.5b).

Apparent-time vs real-time decomposition already run: within-member fixed-effects drift of +0.51 per 1,000 per decade (t = 6.0), ≈40% of total calendar drift, alongside the cohort-replacement component, with the earlier 'incumbents are flat' null explicitly retracted as underpowered (§4.6; Appendix B item 9). This is checklist item 11, and it is done to the standard Sankoff & Blondeau set.

US series extended to a uniform 60 sitting days/year, 1994–2026, both chambers unbroken with no missing year, 780 day-zips, with the sampling scheme's cost correctly characterised as precision not validity (footnote r45c).
Full artifact and code release under analysis/s10 with per-number script and invocation footnotes (Appendix C).

gaps.gap: The 'predates by decades' claim rests on three chambers, not nineteen, and the dated onset rests on one. Only UK Commons (to 1985) and US House/Senate (from 1994) hold pre-2006 data; the other sixteen chambers' pre-model window is 2006–2022, which is sixteen years, not decades. Worse, US House and Senate start AT 1994 and so cannot see a turn, and their long-window trends are +0.4%/yr and +0.5%/yr — essentially flat. So the long-window evidence is one steeply-rising series (UK, +4.3%/yr) plus two flat-and-high series, and the sentence 'level series rising from 1994–96 across chambers' is not what the tables in §4.5a show. What they show is convergence on a level the US already held. A referee reading the table before the prose will flag this as overclaim.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Restate the claim to the two things the data carry: (a) the register level was already at its modern value in the US in 1994, and (b) sixteen chambers converged upward on it. Then either (i) extend at least two more chambers behind 1994 so the onset is replicated — UK is already at 1985; Canadian provincial and Australian state Hansards have pre-1994 print/scanned volumes — or (ii) keep the onset as a single-series UK result and label it so in §4.5's topic sentence and the abstract.
gaps.feasibility: Restatement is free and should happen regardless. Extending chambers behind 1994 is new collection: Canadian provincial and Australian state pre-1994 Hansards are largely scanned print, so this is an acquisition-plus-OCR project, not a re-run.

gaps.gap: Marker-list selection is endogenous to the claim, and the placebos do not control for it. The marker list was selected because those words jumped after 2022. If words that jump in 2022 are disproportionately words that were already rising 1994–2022 — which is exactly what S10's own thesis predicts, since the same drift shaped the training corpus — then running the list backwards manufactures an upward pre-period slope. The 200 placebo sets are matched on frequency and dispersion but not on pre-period trend, so they cannot null this out. This is the checklist's item 7 and it is the one a methods referee will lead with, because it makes the headline finding potentially circular.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Two analyses. (1) Trend-matched placebos: rebuild the placebo pool matched on (frequency, dispersion, 1994–2010 log-rate slope) and re-report the gap series and the 1994 turning point against it. (2) A pre-period-blind marker list: re-derive excess vocabulary from the post-2022 jump after residualising each candidate word on its own 1985/1994–2022 trend, and show the onset and the chamber ordering survive on that list. Also cheap and discriminating: report whether the 1994–96 onset appears on BOTH marker sets the study already holds (Kobak rare-style and the Wikipedia 'signs of AI writing' set) — §4.5 currently contrasts them only for the post-2023 jump, never for the 30-year series.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable from data already held — per-word yearly counts exist in occurrence_trends.json and the trend caches. One to two days. The two-list cross-check is hours.

gaps.gap: Within-chamber genre composition over 30 years is never held fixed. §4.3 establishes the register concentrates in scripted business (SO31 32.3% vs Oral Questions 9.8%, 3.29×). If the scripted share of the record rose after the mid-1990s — and in most Westminster chambers it did, via timetabling reform, members'-statement slots, Westminster Hall from 1999, and longer ministerial statements — the aggregate rate rises with nobody's register changing. The study's fixed-composition work is across chambers, not across years within a chamber, and genre labels exist for exactly one corpus (federal Canada, entering in 2015). This is checklist item 2, it is the control Morin & Acerbi ran and Pechenick's critique was built on, and it is the highest-value missing analysis.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Three tiers, cheapest first. (1) Today: post-stratify each chamber-year to a fixed segment-length distribution and re-run the series — register and flag rate both rise with length, so length-mix drift is a measurable proxy for genre-mix drift, and this converts a hand-wave into a number. (2) Parse order-of-business/debate-title headings out of the raw Hansard and Congressional Record markup for UK Commons and US House/Senate (the Record has structured section headings; Hansard has debate titles), build a coarse three-to-five-way rubric, reweight each year to a fixed composition, and re-run the 1994–2026 series and the turning-point bootstrap. (3) Report a within-genre series for one genre present in every year of the long window.
gaps.feasibility: (1) computable today from held data. (2) computable from held raw files but needs new parsing per chamber — the study explicitly flags US per-segment genre recovery as not-done (§8.6). (3) falls out of (2).

gaps.gap: No per-word decomposition of the 30-year rise. The claim is carried entirely by a pooled aggregate rate. Referees in this literature do not accept that: Morin & Acerbi's paper turns on showing the aggregate decline lives in one subset, and Michel et al. plotted per-word series beside every aggregate. As it stands, nothing rules out a handful of markers — 'delivery', 'framework', 'robust', 'sustainable', 'engagement', 'stakeholder' — carrying the whole 1994–2026 rise, which would relabel the finding as New Public Management vocabulary rather than register.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Per-marker 1994–2026 log-rate slope for every word in the instrument; report the fraction with positive slope, a sign test and Wilcoxon against the placebo pool's slope distribution, the aggregate recomputed with the ten largest contributors trimmed, and a types-per-speech series (distinct markers used) alongside the token rate to show the rise is breadth not repetition. Publish the per-word slope table as a supplement.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from held per-word yearly counts. Hours, not days. This is the cheapest gap on the list and closes the largest rhetorical hole.

gaps.gap: The instrument's American tilt confounds the study's own headline level comparison. §4.5a reports post-training preference correlating with log(US/UK) at ρ = +0.081 and treats that as a finding; but any variety tilt in the marker list also raises US chambers' measured level by construction, and 'the US already held the level in 1994' is a cross-variety level comparison. The orthographic stratum (spelling pairs, 'percent') is reported separately, but lexical-preference tilt is not removed.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Rebuild the instrument on the subset of markers showing no US/UK frequency differential in the 2006–10 reference corpora the study already holds (US 37.6M, UK 44.2M words) — e.g. drop any marker whose |log(US/UK)| exceeds a threshold — then re-run the 1994 and 2026 level tables and report how much of the US–UK level gap survives. Report the survival curve across thresholds rather than one cut.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable today from held reference corpora and per-word counts. Half a day.

gaps.gap: Placebo matching is anchored to one chamber-window and applied 19 chambers wide and 32 years deep. The instrument and its 200 matched placebo sets are built on UK Commons 2010–12. Frequency and dispersion matching degrades with distance from that anchor, and the residual of that degradation is exactly the quantity being reported as 'the gap'. Since the UK is also the fastest riser and the anchor sits mid-series, the anchor choice is not innocent with respect to the convergence result.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Re-derive chamber-specific (and, for the three long chambers, era-specific) matched placebo pools from each chamber's own earliest available window; re-run the growth table and the onset bootstrap; report the rank correlation of the chamber growth ordering between anchor choices. If the ordering is anchor-stable, say so with the number.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from held data — the matching machinery already exists. One day.

gaps.gap: Transcription-regime control is two markers and carries no against-the-original or documentary validation. Mollin 2007 is the governing standard for this corpus and shows Hansard editing removes roughly 75% of emphatic adjectives — precisely the stance vocabulary a register instrument reads — with editorial practice changing over time. Two surface markers (words/sentence, contraction density) cannot detect a style-guide change that touches vocabulary. The study concedes this in Limits ('uses two convention-tracking markers, not all of them'); a referee will treat the concession as the finding.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: (a) Widen the diagnostic panel per chamber-year: honorific and address forms ('hon. Member', 'the Honourable'), reporting-verb inventory, paragraph and sentence-length distributions, interjection and interruption markers, first-person-plural rate, mean words per speech — then show the 1994–96 turn coincides with no step in any of them. (b) Assemble, from each chamber's own style guides, Official Report annual reports and procedure-committee records, the dates of production changes (electronic typesetting, in-house vs contracted reporting, ASR adoption) and overlay them on the gap series.
gaps.feasibility: (a) computable today from held text, one day. (b) new documentary collection, but cheap and public — and it is specifically what a corpus-linguistics referee asks for.

gaps.gap: Digitisation provenance is not stated per chamber-year, and no OCR-quality proxy is reported. US Congressional Record on GovInfo is born-digital from 1994, but pre-2000 Canadian provincial and Australian state Hansards are frequently OCR'd print, and OCR error rates change with scanning campaign — a well-known driver of spurious diachronic trends (Michel et al. discarded most scans for exactly this; Lansdall-Welfare et al. PNAS 2017 carry it as a standing caveat). Silence on this in a paper whose whole claim is a 30-year lexical trend reads as an unexamined threat.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: A per-chamber-year OCR proxy — out-of-vocabulary token rate, or dictionary-hit rate against a fixed lexicon — plotted against the gap series, with the correlation reported; plus a one-paragraph per-source statement of digitisation provenance and a flag or exclusion for any year whose OOV rate steps. Include a residualised series (gap net of OOV rate) as a robustness line.
gaps.feasibility: Computable in an afternoon from held text. The provenance statement needs a short documentary check per chamber.

gaps.gap: The standing named rival — informalization/conversationalization of public discourse — is not confronted with its own instrument. Fairclough (1992) dates the marketization/conversationalization of institutional discourse to the same window S10 dates its onset, and Pearce (2005, Language and Literature 14(1)) measures it in UK political broadcasts 1966–97 with 28 Longman-grammar markers and finds a general rise. S10's formality control is data-defined, exists in three chambers only, and is reported as a single scalar gap. A referee from this field will say the paper has rediscovered informalization under a new name and not tested against it.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Implement a multi-feature formality/involvement dimension per chamber-year across the full 1994–2026 window — either Pearce's 28 markers or a Biber-style informational-vs-involved dimension from surface counts — and report (i) its own trend per chamber, (ii) its correlation with the register gap series, and (iii) the register gap's trend net of it. If the register gap survives conditioning on the informalization dimension, that is the result the section needs; if it does not, better to find out now.
gaps.feasibility: Computable today — every feature is surface-countable from held text, no model needed. Two to three days including feature implementation. Highest ratio of referee-credibility gained to work required, after the per-word decomposition.

gaps.gap: No replication of the 30-year drift outside legislatures. Every strong work in this literature replicates outside its discovery frame (Morin & Acerbi's two metadata-rich corpora; Baker's four matched reference corpora). S10's replication is 19 chambers of the same text type collected the same way, which controls chamber but not corpus.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Run the identical fixed ruler and matched placebos on one non-legislative institutional-English corpus spanning 1994–2026. Best candidate: EDGAR 10-K MD&A sections — free, bulk-downloadable, born-digital from the mid-1990s, and a written-accountability-without-authorship register by construction, which is the paper's own mechanism. Alternates: the UN General Debate Corpus (1946–2024, released, spoken-institutional), or COHA/NOW for general written English. A matching onset outside legislatures makes the claim general; its absence localises it, which is also a publishable result.
gaps.feasibility: New collection, but public, free and scriptable. EDGAR bulk retrieval plus MD&A extraction is roughly a week; the scoring reuses existing code unchanged.

gaps.gap: 'Kobak's excess-vocabulary design is blind to steady drift' is asserted from one in-time placebo rather than demonstrated as an estimator property. The in-time placebo shows the estimator fires when it shouldn't; it does not characterise how the two estimators behave under drift, jump, and drift-plus-jump. Since this asymmetry is the paper's methodological contribution, it is worth more than a footnote.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: A short simulation: synthesise corpora at realistic per-year word counts under (i) steady drift, no jump, (ii) jump, no drift, (iii) both, using the real per-word frequency distribution; run the Kobak excess-vocabulary estimator and the fixed-ruler level estimator on each; report each estimator's estimate and its false-positive rate under each generative process. Publish as a methods figure.
gaps.feasibility: Fully computable from held data. One day. Converts a rhetorical claim into a stated operating characteristic and directly supports the paper's positioning against the prior art.

gaps.gap: Dispersion of the rise across speakers and documents is unreported. The gap is a corpus-level rate; nothing shows whether most members moved a little or a few moved a lot. Egbert & Biber (Corpora 14(1), 2019) is the standing citation that a corpus-frequency result without text dispersion is not representative of the discourse domain, and the study's own note that it 'has been bitten three times' by non-clustered standard errors makes this a live vulnerability.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Share of members, and share of speeches, whose marker rate rises across the series; the trend re-estimated as a member-level random-effects meta-analysis with I² rather than a pooled rate; standard errors clustered on member throughout. The member panels built for §4.6 already carry the join keys.
gaps.feasibility: Computable today from held member panels. Under a day.

gaps.gap: The trend claim is summarised by a rank correlation over 19 endpoint pairs, with no per-chamber uncertainty, no pooled effect and no multiplicity handling. The level claim gets Fisher combination over 47 specifications; the trend claim — the one in the title — gets ρ = −0.56 and a count of sixteen-of-nineteen rising.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Per-chamber trend estimate with a day- or session-clustered CI, a random-effects pooled trend with I² and prediction interval, and a stated correction over the chamber family. Report the sixteen-of-nineteen count as a sign test with its p-value rather than as a tally.
gaps.feasibility: Computable today from held series. Hours.

gaps.gap: Age-period-cohort collinearity is not addressed in print. Birth year, calendar year and tenure are exactly linearly dependent; §4.6's split of a standing juniority gradient from a cohort component requires an identifying restriction, and apc_chamber_decomposition.py's is not stated in the text. Any reviewer who has met the APC problem will ask, and the juniority-gradient result is load-bearing for 'predates even that'.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: State the identifying restriction explicitly, show the result's sensitivity to it (at minimum: two alternative restrictions, and the intrinsic-estimator or constrained-regression comparison), and frame the decomposition against Sankoff & Blondeau (Language 83(3), 2007) so the panel/trend distinction is the reader's frame.
gaps.feasibility: Computable today; the restriction is already implicit in existing code. Half a day plus prose.

surveys.verdict: S10 exceeds the field standard on the two controls this literature was built by attacking — a ruler fixed independently of the years it measures, and a frequency-and-dispersion-matched placebo null, plus a transcription-regime diagnostic most parliamentary-corpus work skips — but falls short of it on four items a corpus-linguistics referee treats as automatic: within-chamber genre-composition reweighting, per-word decomposition of an aggregate word-list rate, a formal break test behind a dated onset that currently rests on a single chamber's series, and the fact that the marker list was selected on the very outcome the backward projection claims to find; all four are computable from data already held, and until they are run the headline sentence claims more chambers and more decades than the tables in §4.5a support.

nearest_works.work: Mrinank Sharma et al., "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models" (arXiv:2310.13548)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: A specific behaviour (sycophancy) is installed by the human-preference stage of training, and is driven by imperfections in the preference signal itself.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: (1) Behavioural prevalence across 5 assistants (Claude 1.3/2.0, GPT-3.5/4, Llama-2-70B-chat) x 4 free-form tasks. (2) TRAINING-SIGNAL evidence: Bayesian logistic regression over text-labeled features on the hh-rlhf preference data, showing 'matches user's beliefs' is among the most predictive features of a human preference judgment. (3) INTERVENTION + DOSE-RESPONSE: best-of-N sampling and RL against the actual preference model used to train Claude 2, sweeping optimization strength and tracking sycophancy as a function of it. (4) Human-vs-PM comparison on the same responses. (5) Honest mixed reporting: some forms of sycophancy rise under PM optimization, others fall.

nearest_works.work: Tom S. Juzek & Zina B. Ward, "Why Does ChatGPT 'Delve' So Much? Exploring the Sources of Lexical Overrepresentation in LLMs" (arXiv:2412.11385); follow-up "Word Overuse and Alignment in LLMs: The Influence of Learning from Human Feedback" (arXiv:2508.01930)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: The overused vocabulary ('delve', 'intricate', 'underscore') is not inherited from pretraining frequency but induced by learning from human feedback.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Ruled out the competing explanation first (training-data frequency does not track the overuse). Then log-prob/surprisal comparison: the human-preference-trained model is less surprised by buzzword-bearing abstracts than the base model that lacked preference training. Then, crucially, went to the SIGNAL: a human-subject experiment showing annotators systematically prefer text variants containing the words — closing the annotator-preference -> model-preference loop rather than stopping at the base/instruct correlation. Public code and data; stated limitation about annotator-population generalization.

nearest_works.work: Bill Yuchen Lin et al., "The Unlocking Spell on Base LLMs: Rethinking Alignment via In-Context Learning" (URIAL, arXiv:2312.01552)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Alignment tuning installs style/discourse form, not knowledge — the superficial-alignment claim in its measured form.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Position-resolved token-distribution-shift analysis between base and aligned models on matched decoding, showing base and aligned agree on most token positions and that shift concentrates on stylistic tokens (discourse markers, disclaimers), across multiple base/aligned pairs (Llama-2, Llama-2-chat, Mistral, Mistral-Instruct, Llama-2-70b-chat). Then a SUFFICIENCY demonstration: 3 constant stylistic in-context examples plus a system prompt on the UNTUNED base reproduce or exceed SFT and SFT+RLHF behaviour — i.e. they produced the effect without the training stage.

nearest_works.work: Constantinos Karouzos, Xingwei Tan & Nikolaos Aletras, "Where does output diversity collapse in post-training?" (arXiv:2604.16027)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Localizes a behavioural change (diversity collapse) to specific post-training stages — the same claim shape as S10 — and explicitly indicts prior stage-attribution work.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Their stated critique of prior work is the design requirement: 'Prior work attributes collapse to specific post-training methods, without separating the role of training data composition from the method, or the generation format from the model weights.' Their answer: THREE PARALLEL post-training lineages of Olmo 3 (Think / Instruct / RL-Zero) so data composition varies independently of method; 15 tasks x 4 diversity metrics; an inference-time intervention (suppressing CoT) to prove the effect is in weights not format; and a decomposition of the loss into a quality-control component and a residual component. Finding: the LOCATION OF COLLAPSE CO-VARIES WITH DATA COMPOSITION, not with the algorithm — SFT is where Think collapses, DPO matters more in Instruct.

nearest_works.work: Aniket Anand, Janvijay Singh, Zhewei Sun, Dilek Hakkani-Tur & Nick Feamster, "Measuring, Localizing, and Ablating Alignment Signatures in LLMs" (PASTA, arXiv:2605.30526)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Post-training installs the stylistic signature that AI-text detectors key on — S10's claim, stated on the model side.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Matched-prefix comparison of human / base-model / aligned-model generations; detection rates from 6 independent AI detectors; then CAUSAL localization — residual contrasts between aligned and base identify alignment directions, which are ablated at decoding across 11 aligned models, showing detectability drops while relevance is preserved. Random-direction negative controls. Cross-detector transfer validation. This is the current bar: an intervention that removes the effect, not just a delta that measures it.

nearest_works.work: Xiaoyi Li, "Do Post-Training Algorithms Actually Differ? A Controlled Study Across Model Scales Uncovers Scale-Dependent Ranking Inversions" (arXiv:2603.19335)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Not a behaviour-attribution paper — the field's current statement of the variance floor that any stage/algorithm comparison must clear.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: ~240 H100 runs; 51 algorithms; core comparison 8 algorithms x 4 scales (Qwen-2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B); 20 DPO variants x 5 seeds = 100 runs at 1.5B. Reports seed sigma 0.22–1.77 pp at 1.5B and 2.01 pp for DPO at 3B, and shows algorithm rankings INVERT across model scale. Also documents a DistributedSampler seed-propagation bug that silently zeroed out seed variance in their own pipeline — i.e. an apparent clean stage difference can be an artifact of a broken seed. Conclusion: single-run comparisons between post-training stages are unreliable.

field_standard: Stage-resolved measurement on a public, checkpointed ladder where every stage shares one base and one prompt set — the entry ticket, not the claim.
Replication across >=3 independent model families, reported PER FAMILY, not only pooled (Sharma 5 assistants; Juzek 6 families; Anand 11 aligned models).
A pre-committed negative-control stage or condition the design predicts should be null, PLUS null calibration of the estimator itself on random/frequency-matched items.

Separate the training OBJECTIVE from the training DATA: two stages that differ in loss almost always differ in corpus. Accepted move is parallel lineages holding one constant (Karouzos 2026), or re-running a stage on swapped data.
Separate model WEIGHTS from generation FORMAT: matched decoding, matched template, and ideally an inference-time manipulation showing the effect survives format changes (Karouzos CoT-suppression).

A sufficiency OR intervention arm — one of: produce the effect without the stage (URIAL 3-shot on base; Singhal's length-only reward), remove it by ablation with random-direction controls (PASTA), or retrain with the stage's data ablated.
Dose-response in optimization pressure: effect measured as a monotone function of RL steps or best-of-N strength (Perez 2023 varying RL steps; Sharma's BoN sweep), not two endpoints.
Seed / run variance: >=3 seeds per stage, or an explicit power statement with a minimum detectable effect. Post-Li-2026 this is a named norm and a null from one run is not reportable as a null.

Length/verbosity control on the headline effect — length is the single most-documented confound in preference-stage attributions (Singhal, COLM 2024: a purely length-based reward reproduces most downstream RLHF gains).

Evidence from the TRAINING SIGNAL itself: show the preference pairs or reward model actually favour the behaviour (Sharma's hh-rlhf regression; Juzek & Ward's human preference experiment). This is what converts 'appears after stage S' into 'is what S rewards'.

Distinguish INTRODUCED from merely AMPLIFIED — the model-diffing literature's central failure mode (Minder et al., arXiv:2504.02922: naive L1 crosscoders misattribute concepts as fine-tuning-introduced when they exist in both models; hence Latent Scaling / BatchTopK).
Released artifacts: named checkpoint revisions, generations, prompts, seeds, code.
Explicit scoping of what is and is not claimed (association vs identified mechanism), and honest reporting of mixed-direction or under-powered sub-results.
we_meet: Stage-resolved ladder on a public checkpointed lineage with same prompts across stages — OLMo-2, SFT/DPO/RLVR plus end-to-end base->instruct +1.24 (§4.7, olmo_ladder.py).

Cross-family replication for the pooled alignment effect: 3-4 families, 1,600 prompt pairs each, 1.19M base words, reported per family (+0.356 to +0.749 pooled) rather than only as a pool (rlhf_pref_compile.py).

Pre-committed negative-control stage: RLVR designed as the placebo, and corrected it behaves as one (+0.06, CI straddles 0) — the design's own manipulation check, which the shipped estimator had failed.

Null calibration of the estimator itself, at a standard above the field median: 30 random frequency-matched word lists return +0.003 under the estimator used, versus +0.45 under the naive variant — with both flaws (control draw universe, bucketing denominator) named and shown to be load-bearing.

Control-pedestal (M3) correction with three independent corrected routes agreeing, plus an additivity check that closes the +1.99-vs-+1.24 stage-sum gap to ~0.03 — internal-consistency evidence most stage-attribution papers do not offer.
Prompt-level uncertainty on the key contrast: paired bootstrap over 800 shared prompts, DPO - SFT = -0.08, 95% CI [-0.31, +0.15], reported as indistinguishable rather than as an ordering.

Convergence-of-estimator diagnostic: well-measured estimate flat under doubling (+0.3881 -> +0.3903) while the pooled estimate keeps climbing — and the draft instructs quoting the well-measured figure.
Explicit non-claims: 'an association, not an identified mechanism', and the section's argument explicitly no longer rests on the stage attribution.

Honest flagging of the weak sub-result rather than burial: the 30B MoE family at +0.067 well-measured with only 37 style words clearing 20 occurrences, called 'an unresolved flag, not a counter-result'.
Committed log-probs, named scripts and invocations, reproducible from analysis/s10/.

gaps.gap: OBJECTIVE vs DATA confound at RLVR — the load-bearing one. On the OLMo-2/Tulu-3 ladder, SFT and DPO train on chat demonstrations and preference pairs (text saturated with the register) while RLVR trains on math/code prompts under verifiable reward. RLVR's null is equally well explained by 'its training text contains no register to install' as by 'verifiable-correctness objectives do not install register'. S10's sentence — 'not by the stage tuned toward verifiable correctness' — is an OBJECTIVE claim the design cannot separate from a DATA claim. Karouzos et al. (arXiv:2604.16027, Apr 2026) name this exact failure as the flaw in prior stage-attribution work and find that collapse location co-varies with data composition, not method. A referee who has read that paper writes this objection in their first paragraph.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Two analyses, both cheap. (a) Run the register ruler over the Olmo 3 RL-Zero lineage — verifiable-reward RL applied from base with no SFT/DPO — which is the only public configuration that isolates the objective. Compare against the Think and Instruct lineages (Karouzos's exact design, public checkpoints). (b) Score the Tulu-3 SFT targets and the RLVR prompt/verifier set with the same ruler and report register density in each; if SFT targets are high and RLVR prompts near zero, that QUANTIFIES the data explanation instead of leaving it as an unaddressed alternative. If (a) shows RL-Zero also null, the objective claim survives; if not, reword to 'installed by the stages trained on human-written chat text' — a data claim, which the current design does support.
gaps.feasibility: No new collection. Public Olmo 3 lineage checkpoints + public Tulu-3 mixture + the existing ruler. Days.

gaps.gap: The stage-resolved result is n=1 run on n=1 family, and its headline finding is a NULL. 'RLVR ~ 0' and 'SFT indistinguishable from DPO' are both single-lineage, single-seed measurements. The paired bootstrap resamples PROMPTS, which quantifies measurement noise but says nothing about run-to-run variance. Li (arXiv:2603.19335, Mar 2026) reports DPO seed sigma of 2.01 pp at 3B, rankings inverting across scale, and — most damagingly — a DistributedSampler bug that made seed variance silently vanish, meaning an apparently clean stage difference can be a pipeline artifact. A null from one run with no minimum-detectable-effect is not currently reportable as a null in this literature.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Three options, in ascending cost. (a) Cheapest and highest value: Ai2 releases OLMo-2 RLVR intermediate checkpoints every 20 steps on HuggingFace revisions — run the ruler across 40+ of them and report register as a trajectory. A flat trajectory across the whole RLVR run is far stronger evidence than one endpoint, and it doubles as the dose-response arm (G3). (b) Replicate the ladder at a second scale/lineage (OLMo-2 1B DPO and Instruct, OLMo-2 32B, Olmo 3 Instruct are all released) — cross-lineage rather than cross-seed, but it is what is publicly obtainable without training. (c) State the minimum detectable effect explicitly: back out from the existing bootstrap SE what size RLVR effect the design could have detected, and report RLVR as 'below X', never as 'zero'.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from public checkpoints plus S10's existing pipeline. (a) is inference-only and is the single best value-per-GPU-hour item on this list.

gaps.gap: No dose-response anywhere in the arm. Perez et al. (ACL Findings 2023) varied the number of RL steps; Sharma et al. (ICLR 2024) swept best-of-N optimization strength against the actual Claude-2 preference model. In this literature, monotonicity in optimization pressure is the move that lifts a stage association toward a mechanism, and S10 explicitly disclaims mechanism partly because it lacks this. Three endpoint deltas cannot distinguish 'the preference objective installs the register' from 'the register happened to be in the checkpoint at that point in the pipeline'.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Best-of-N sweep against an open reward model (Tulu-3's or Skywork RM) applied to the BASE-model generations S10 has already produced: re-rank the existing samples at N = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and plot register excess against N. If register rises monotonically with N, the preference signal itself demonstrably rewards the register — which is the arm that would let S10 upgrade its own explicit non-claim. Pair with the per-20-step RLVR checkpoint sweep from G2(a) for the negative half of the dose-response.
gaps.feasibility: From data S10 already holds (generations + log-probs) plus one downloadable open reward model. No new collection; re-ranking is cheap because generation is already done.

gaps.gap: No evidence from the training signal itself — the gap that most sharply separates S10 from its two nearest neighbours. Sharma et al. regressed human preference on text features over hh-rlhf; Juzek & Ward ran a human-subject preference experiment and showed annotators genuinely prefer the overused words. Both went to the DATA that defines the stage. S10 measures only model outputs on both sides of the stage boundary. The obvious referee question — 'do the preference pairs that trained this model actually favour the higher-register response?' — is unanswered, and it is answerable.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: The Tulu-3 preference mixture is public. Compute register excess on chosen vs rejected within each pair; report (i) the paired within-pair difference with a bootstrap CI, (ii) the win-rate of the higher-register member of each pair, (iii) both with length residualized, since chosen responses skew longer. Optionally extend to the SFT targets vs the base model's own completions on the same prompts. This is a single script against the existing ruler and it is the highest-value single addition in the list: it is the mechanism evidence, and unlike G1 and G2 it requires no checkpoint downloads at all.
gaps.feasibility: Public data + existing ruler. No new collection. Hours.

gaps.gap: Length is not controlled in the headline effect. S10 already found length biting: the control pedestal was 'largest at DPO only because DPO's generations are longest'. The M3 correction removes the ESTIMATOR's length-driven bias but does not produce a length-controlled EFFECT — a genuine register delta could still be substantially a verbosity delta. Singhal et al. (COLM 2024) established that a purely length-based reward reproduces most downstream RLHF improvements over SFT and that reward models are the dominant source of the bias, which makes length the first confound any referee tests in a preference-stage attribution.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Two recomputations on generations S10 already holds: (a) truncate every generation to the shortest common length within its prompt pair and recompute all stage deltas and the +0.387; (b) regress per-prompt register excess on stage indicator with log(token count) as a covariate, reporting the stage coefficient. Report both next to the headline. If the effect survives at similar magnitude, this closes a whole line of attack for one afternoon's work; if it shrinks, better to find that internally.
gaps.feasibility: Entirely from data S10 already holds. Cheap.

gaps.gap: base-vs-instruct (+1.24) is confounded with chat template and decoding regime, and the sufficiency arm is missing. The comparison runs a base model on raw prompts against an instruct model in its chat format. Karouzos et al. make weights-vs-generation-format a named design requirement; Lin et al. (URIAL, ICLR 2024) showed that THREE in-context stylistic examples on the untuned base recover most of alignment's stylistic behaviour. If a URIAL-style 3-shot prefix on OLMo-2 base reproduces a large share of +1.24, the honest claim narrows from 'post-training installs the register' to 'post-training makes the register the unprompted default' — a real and defensible claim, but not the one currently written.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Four arms on the same prompt set: (1) base, raw; (2) base with a 3-shot URIAL-style stylistic prefix carrying no register vocabulary in the exemplars themselves; (3) instruct with chat template; (4) instruct WITHOUT chat template. Report the share of the +1.24 that each arm recovers. This is the cheapest arm on the list that could actually change the sentence, so it should be run before the sentence is finalized rather than after review.
gaps.feasibility: From models and prompts S10 already runs. Inference only. Cheap.

gaps.gap: No causal localization, and no test of INTRODUCED vs merely AMPLIFIED. The 2026 frontier for this exact claim is an intervention: Anand et al. (PASTA) ablate the base-vs-aligned residual contrast direction across 11 models and show detector rates fall, with random-direction controls. Separately, Minder et al. (arXiv:2504.02922) established the model-diffing community's central caution — naive crosscoders MISATTRIBUTE concepts as introduced by fine-tuning when they in fact exist in both models, which is why Latent Scaling and BatchTopK exist. That failure mode is the interpretability analogue of S10's own pedestal defect, so a referee who knows it will ask whether post-training INTRODUCED the register direction or merely amplified a preference the base model already had — which, given that S10's whole thesis is that the register predates the machines, is a question S10 has an unusually strong reason to want answered.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Split into a cheap half and an expensive half. CHEAP (do this one): from the base-model log-probs S10 already holds, test whether the BASE model already ranks register words above frequency-matched controls at the same token positions. A positive result says post-training amplified a pre-existing preference rather than creating one — which strengthens, not weakens, the paper's central historical claim, and costs nothing. EXPENSIVE: compute the base-vs-instruct residual contrast on S10's paired generations, ablate it at decoding, re-run both the register ruler and Pangram, with random-direction negative controls (the PASTA recipe).
gaps.feasibility: The amplified-vs-introduced check is computable from data S10 already holds, today. The activation ablation needs new GPU work but no new data collection.

gaps.gap: The two headline numbers are not commensurable and the draft says so only in a footnote. +1.24 is one family end-to-end on the OLMo ladder; +0.387 is a SEPARATE experiment on three other families with no stage resolution and a different generation length. A reader of the abstract — and any referee skimming — will take them as one coherent result, and the abstract's phrasing does nothing to stop that. Relatedly, the additivity check (three uncorrected stages sum to +1.99 against +1.24, closing to ~0.03 corrected) is the strongest single piece of evidence that the corrected estimator is unbiased, and it is buried in footnote r47.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Presentational, no new computation. (a) Promote the additivity check into a main-text table as an estimator-validation row. (b) State plainly in §4.7 and in the abstract that stage resolution rests on ONE family and that the cross-family number is end-to-end only. (c) Give the two numbers visually distinct labels so they are never read as a decomposition.
gaps.feasibility: Writing only.

gaps.gap: The 30B MoE family is under-powered on an unmatched budget, flagged but unresolved: its instruct side never passed 800 prompts and only 37 style words clear 20 occurrences, versus 1,600 prompts elsewhere. Per-family reporting is the norm S10 correctly follows (Betley et al., ICML 2025 report per-model with matched budgets; Anand et al. across 11 models), but an unmatched family inside a pooled figure is a hole a referee will pick at — and the draft's own honest flag tells them exactly where to push.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Either finish the instruct side to 1,600 prompts to match the other families, or remove it from the pooled +0.387 and report it separately as an under-powered fourth replication with its own budget stated. The draft already records why the run stalled (MoE active-parameter advantage disappearing at batch 48), so the compute estimate is known; that note is worth keeping either way since it is a genuine and reusable finding.
gaps.feasibility: Compute only, already scoped and costed by the study.

surveys.verdict: S10's estimator hygiene is above the field median — the pre-committed RLVR placebo, the null calibration returning +0.003 against a naive +0.45, three agreeing correction routes, the stage-sum additivity check, and per-family reporting are all better than most of the delve/RLHF-style literature — but the arm meets only the descriptive half of the field's checklist and none of the attribution half: it has no separation of training objective from training data (the exact flaw Karouzos et al. 2026 indict prior work for, and the one that makes the RLVR null ambiguous), no dose-response, no evidence from the preference data itself (which both nearest neighbours, Sharma and Juzek & Ward, treat as the decisive move), no length-controlled effect, and a single run on a single family carrying a null — so as currently worded the claim overshoots its design, though four of the nine gaps (preference-pair scoring, the RLVR per-20-step checkpoint sweep, length control, and the URIAL base-prompting arm) are computable from data and public checkpoints S10 already has access to and would together close the distance.

nearest_works.work: Steenbergen, Bächtiger, Spörndli & Steiner, "Measuring Political Deliberation: A Discourse Quality Index"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: That a Habermas-grounded, behaviourally-anchored index can measure deliberative quality of parliamentary speech reliably enough for downstream analysis — the instrument S10 borrows and whose codings S10 uses as anchors.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Two named coders (Steiner, Steenbergen) independently coded all 56 demand-bearing speeches of one 1998 Commons debate, then reconvened to argue disagreements to resolution. 504 judgments, overall Holsti RCA 0.915. Per-category reliability table: level of justification RCA 0.732 / Cohen's κ 0.615 / Spearman r 0.716 / standardized α 0.834; respect-toward-groups κ 0.746; respect-toward-demands κ 0.844 (r 0.855, n=29 applicable); respect-toward-counterarguments κ 0.559 (r 0.791, only n=5 applicable). Agreement on whether an indicator is *applicable* is reported as a distinct reliability question from agreement on the code. Index construction backed by a polychoric correlation matrix as unidimensionality evidence, with zero-variance components dropped.

nearest_works.work: Gerber, Bächtiger, Shikano, Reber & Rohr, "Deliberative Abilities and Influence in a Transnational Deliberative Poll (EuroPolis)"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: That deliberative ability is measurable at individual level with an updated DQI and is unequally distributed by class — i.e. a substantive claim resting on DQI-coded outcomes, the same claim shape as S10's.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 944 speech acts coded on an updated DQI; unit of analysis explicitly the speech act. Three independent coders; reliability tables in appendix (A3, A4). Critically: when the first reliability test on level and content of justification came back only 'satisfactory', they clarified the disagreements, re-coded the data, and ran a second reliability test — reliability failure on the claim-bearing dimension was remediated, not disclosed-and-kept. Latent ability estimated with an item-response model rather than an equal-weight additive index. Measurement confounds controlled explicitly (a dummy for translated speeches, shown null). Representativeness of the coded subsample checked against all other participants (Table A8).

nearest_works.work: Behrendt, Wagner, Ziegele, Wilms, Stoll, Heinbach & Harmeling, "AQuA — Combining Experts' and Non-Experts' Views To Assess Deliberation Quality in Online Discussions Using LLMs"
nearest_works.venue_year: 1st Workshop on Language-driven Deliberation Technology (DELITE) @ LREC-COLING 2024; arXiv:2404.02761
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: That an automated additive deliberative-quality score can stand in for trained-coder DQI-style coding at scale — the current state of the art in computational deliberation metrics.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 13,069 comments coded by trained coders on 23 deliberative criteria (KODIE / #meinfernsehen); intercoder reliability tested on 130 and 159 comment subsets against an explicit critical threshold of Krippendorff's α = .67, mean α .83 and .74, with the one category failing named. Dimension weights derived empirically from 1,742 comments crowd-annotated by 681 non-experts, not assumed equal. Per-indicator F1 on a held-out 20% test split, reported dimension by dimension and unflattering where deserved (justification F1 29.5, relevance 13.2, respect 69.7). Out-of-distribution transfer demonstrated on two corpora not seen in training (SFU SOCC, and Europolis parliamentary-style speech, where predictions are compared to the original Gerber et al. labels). An explicit length-confound check (Fig. 3: AQuA score vs word count) showing medium-length comments score highest, to rule out length as the driver.

nearest_works.work: Fournier-Tombs & MacKenzie, "Big data and democratic speech: Predicting deliberative quality using machine learning techniques" (with predecessor Fournier-Tombs & Di Marzo Serugendo, "DelibAnalysis", Journal of Information Science 46(6), 2020)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: That a classifier trained on human DQI codings can predict discourse quality for uncoded legislative speech at scale — the direct precedent for automating DQI on Canadian legislatures (Yukon, NWT, Nunavut).
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: A human-coded training set on a simplified 12-indicator DQI 2.0, a supervised classifier trained on those codes, classifier performance stated against held-out human codings, and automated scores used downstream only after that performance is on the record. The framework is pitched as replicable, platform- and language-agnostic, with the human-coded seed as the load-bearing artefact.

nearest_works.work: Egami, Hinck, Stewart & Wei, "Using Imperfect Surrogates for Downstream Inference: Design-based Supervised Learning for Social Science Applications of Large Language Models" (companion: Angelopoulos, Bates, Fannjiang, Jordan & Zrnic, "Prediction-powered inference", Science 382:669–674, 2023)
nearest_works.venue_year: NeurIPS 2023 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36); arXiv:2306.04746
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: That regression coefficients estimated on LLM-produced labels are not valid as reported — the estimation standard for exactly S10's design, where an LLM's DQI score is the dependent variable.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Proof plus simulation that plugging surrogate labels into downstream analyses yields substantial bias and invalid confidence intervals even at 80–90% surrogate accuracy; a doubly-robust DSL estimator that combines surrogates with a *probability-sampled* gold-standard subset with known inclusion probabilities; guarantees that hold when the surrogate is arbitrarily biased; a released R package (`dsl`). The design requirement — that the gold subsample be drawn by a recorded random rule, not by convenience — is the operative constraint.

nearest_works.work: Herbold, Hautli-Janisz, Heuer, Kikteva & Trautsch, "A large-scale comparison of human-written versus ChatGPT-generated essays"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: That machine-written text is rated *higher* in quality than human-written text on a standard rubric — the identical claim shape to S10's 'better-formed, not degraded', in a venue that made it stick.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Domain-expert human raters (secondary-school teachers, 139 registered / 111 completing), a within-subject design giving 658 ratings over 270 essays with 2–3 raters for nearly every essay; a seven-criterion rubric based on content and language mastery; Cronbach's α reported per criterion and per data source (α > 0.9 throughout, 0.89 for language mastery); Wilcoxon tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction across all 42 comparisons; effect sizes as Cohen's d (0.52–1.15); bootstrap CIs; rater self-assessment shown uncorrelated with ratings; and an independent linguistic-feature analysis as convergent, non-rater evidence. (Compare Kreps & Kriner, New Media & Society 26(12), 2024: 32,398 emails to 7,132 US state legislators, AI vs human response rates 15.4% vs 17.3% — political science's other route to this claim is a behavioural outcome under *assigned* provenance, not an inferred one.)

field_standard: Unit of analysis matches the instrument: DQI codes the demand-bearing speech act, not an arbitrary text window (Steenbergen 2003: 56 demand-bearing speeches; Gerber 2018: 944 speech acts). Applicability and justification scores are both unit-dependent, so the segmentation rule is part of the measurement.

Every claim-bearing dimension is double-coded by ≥2 independent coders on a reliability subsample, with chance-corrected per-dimension agreement reported (Cohen's κ, Krippendorff's α), not just raw percent or self-correlation. Published bars: κ 0.559–0.844 (Steenbergen 2003); α ≥ .67 as the critical threshold with the failing category named (Behrendt 2024).

Agreement on whether a conditional indicator is *applicable* is reported separately from agreement on the code given, because respect-toward-demands and respect-toward-counterarguments are conditional and their applicability rate is itself a finding (Steenbergen 2003 states this explicitly; their counterargument dimension had n=5 applicable cases out of 56).
Reliability failure on a claim-bearing dimension is remediated — clarify, re-code, re-test — not merely disclosed (Gerber et al. 2018, fn 77, on level and content of justification).

Human-vs-instrument agreement, never instrument-vs-itself. Test-retest / repeat-pass stability is not accepted as evidence of validity: Desai, Card & Jacobs (arXiv:2607.07915, 2026), surveying LLM-as-measurement papers across eight flagship social-science journals, find convergent validity against a human gold standard is the dominant and expected practice, and flag studies whose gold sets are too small or whose agreement metric is uncorrected for chance. Bavaresco et al. (ACL 2025, JUDGE-BENCH, 20 datasets / 11 LLMs) conclude judges must be validated against human judgments per task before use.

If an automated coder replaces trained coders, report its per-dimension performance against held-out human codes, plus performance on at least one corpus not used in development (Fournier-Tombs & MacKenzie 2021; Behrendt 2024's SOCC and Europolis transfer tests, with per-adapter F1 published including the bad ones).

When a machine label is the outcome or regressor in a downstream estimate, correct the estimate for label error using a probability-sampled gold-standard subset — DSL (Egami et al., NeurIPS 2023) or PPI (Angelopoulos et al., Science 2023). Plug-in surrogate estimates are treated as biased with invalid CIs even at 80–90% accuracy.

Judge-specific bias audits for LLM raters: self-recognition/self-preference (Panickssery, Bowman & Feng, NeurIPS 2024 — a measured linear relation between a model's self-recognition ability and how much it over-scores its own output), verbosity/position bias, and a cross-family judge as the standard robustness replication.

Prompt and codebook robustness: Halterman & Keith, "Codebook LLMs: Evaluating LLMs as Measurement Tools for Political Science Concepts", Political Analysis 34(2):188–204, 2026, show LLM codebook classifiers are sensitive to codebook element ordering, lean on label semantics over stipulated definitions, fail at exclusion criteria, and lean on lexical overlap; they prescribe label-free behavioural tests and explicit error analysis before hand-labelling investment.

Composite construction is justified rather than assumed: polychoric correlations for unidimensionality (Steenbergen 2003), IRT latent scoring (Gerber 2018), or empirically-derived weights (Behrendt 2024). Equal weighting is a defensible default only with an argument attached.
Multiple-comparison correction across dimensions and effect sizes in interpretable units (Herbold 2023: Holm-Bonferroni over 42 tests, Cohen's d reported for every significant contrast).

Length/verbosity treated as a first-class threat, since DQI justification and LLM judges both reward length; the standard is an explicit score-vs-length analysis (Behrendt 2024, Fig. 3), not a covariate footnote.
For a null claim ('no less engaged'), report power/MDE at minimum, and preferably equivalence bounds against a pre-specified smallest effect of interest.
we_meet: Instrument provenance and content validity: the rubric is the DQI proper (Steenbergen, Bächtiger, Spörndli & Steiner 2003) with the original authors' own published codings of the 1998 Commons women's-issues debate used as in-context calibration anchors — the scale is the instrument authors', not the judge's invention. Stronger anchoring than most automated-DQI work, which retrains on fresh labels.

Applicability handled correctly and as its own quantity: the −1 inapplicable code is excluded from means rather than scored zero, the reason is argued (scoring 'nothing to engage with' as worse than 'engaged badly' would manufacture the engagement penalty), and the applicability collapse is reported as a separate finding with its own numbers (respect_demands applicable 61.4% / 63.0% / 31.1% by screen band, n = 498/297/45; respect_counterargs 50.8 / 51.2 / 28.9%). This is the one thing Steenbergen 2003 insists on that most successors drop.
Per-dimension reliability reported and benchmarked against the instrument's own published bar (repeat-pass Spearman 0.68–0.91 vs Steenbergen's inter-coder r = 0.716 on justification).

Two label sources over two different populations converging: stage 1 (840 genre-balanced federal-Canadian segments, blinded LLM screen score) and stage 2 (682 segments across 22 chambers, external Pangram verdict, chamber FE) give the same signs and comparable per-sd magnitudes. An external-label arm is more than the automated-DQI precedents provide.

Confounds diagnosed rather than adjusted away: the 'deliberation down' result is shown to be genre (uncontrolled respect_demands −0.662 t −2.4 → null under genre FE), and the justification lift is correctly identified as a suppression effect (SO31 concentrates machine drafting and has the lowest justification of any genre, 1.10 vs 2.09).

Length decomposed rather than partialled silently: within-chamber log-length control gives justification +0.290 → +0.157 (t 2.4), respect_groups length-free (+0.220 → +0.222), common_good +0.229 → +0.199, and evidence's marginal +0.065 shown to be entirely length (→ −0.017). This meets the AQuA-style length check.

Speaker-clustered standard errors on every claim-bearing cell (no claim-bearing t moves by more than 0.3), and Benjamini-Hochberg across the 14 cells with the one cell that fails (respect_groups, q = 0.106) starred-with-disclosure rather than quietly retained.

The judge-leakage diagnostic was specified, actually run, and reported (Appendix D.1) with the two largest conjuncts surviving on the external label (justification t 3.6, common_good t 3.2) — and with an argued case that the control is a collider/collinear bad control rather than a suppressed result.
Nulls carry MDE statements, and the evasion arms are within-text paired (63 pairs), which fixes content, speaker and occasion by construction.
Full computational reproducibility: id-keyed per-grade rows committed (stage1/2_grades_by_id.json), scripts named per number, exact multiset re-derivation recorded.

gaps.gap: No human-coded gold standard anywhere in the quality arm. Not one DQI code in the study was produced by a person; every reliability figure is the judge agreeing with itself across passes. Both surveyed literatures treat human agreement as the entry ticket, not a nicety — the DQI tradition because chance-corrected inter-coder κ/α *is* the instrument's warrant (Steenbergen 2003 Table 1; Gerber 2018's re-code-and-retest), and the LLM-judge tradition because self-consistency is exactly what a systematically biased judge also produces (Desai, Card & Jacobs 2026; Bavaresco et al. ACL 2025). The draft already concedes the point in three places ('the human-coded subsample remains the real validation'), which means a referee will read the concession as a self-identified blocker.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Two trained coders independently code a stratified random subsample of the stage-2 pool — stratify on Pangram verdict × genre × chamber, with the draw made by a recorded random rule and inclusion probabilities logged (this is also the precondition for gap 2). 150–200 segments buys per-dimension Cohen's κ with usable CIs; the two conditional dimensions must be oversampled on applicable cases or they will replicate Steenbergen's n=5 problem. Report per-dimension Krippendorff α, applicability agreement separately from code agreement, and κ between each human and the LLM judge. Where a dimension comes back below α .67, follow Gerber: clarify the rubric, re-code, re-test, and say so.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds — the segments and the grades exist. The missing input is human coder time, not new corpus collection: roughly two coders × one week including training on the Steenbergen anchors. This is the single largest cost item on the list and the only one that cannot be bought with API credits.

gaps.gap: +0.29 sd is a plug-in estimate on surrogate labels, so both the point estimate and its confidence interval are of unknown validity. Egami et al. (NeurIPS 2023) show directly that regressing on LLM-produced labels gives substantial bias and invalid CIs even when the surrogate is 80–90% accurate — and S10 has no accuracy number at all for its judge. The sign of the finding may be robust; the number quoted in the abstract is not yet a number a methods referee will let stand unqualified.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Re-estimate the stage-2 regressions with design-based supervised learning (the `dsl` R package) or prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al. 2023), using gap 1's probability-sampled gold subset. Report the bias-corrected coefficient and valid CI alongside the plug-in estimate, and state the direction and size of the correction. If the corrected estimate is materially smaller, the abstract sentence changes from a magnitude claim to a sign claim — which is still publishable, and honest.
gaps.feasibility: Pure re-analysis once gap 1 exists; hours of work. But it is gated on gap 1 being drawn as a probability sample — if the human subsample is chosen by convenience (e.g. 'the interesting cases'), DSL/PPI cannot be applied and the gap stays open. Design the sample for this now.

gaps.gap: Detector-side selection on quality is untested, and it is the first objection any referee will raise: the treatment variable is a detector's verdict, and a detector that keys on fluent, well-formed, low-perplexity prose will preferentially flag well-formed text regardless of provenance. The 1,260/1,260 pre-2022 specificity bounds false positives at the *threshold* but says nothing about whether the underlying score is correlated with form. If it is, part of '+0.29 sd more justified' is the instrument selecting on the outcome.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Run the placebo that the study's own design makes available: on the pre-2022 calibration corpus, where every text is human by construction, grade a sample on the same v2b rubric and regress each DQI dimension on the continuous Pangram score and on the continuous screen score, with genre and chamber FE. A null slope on pre-2022 human text is a clean identification argument for the wild contrast; a positive slope gives a direct numerical bound on how much of the +0.29 is detector selection rather than drafting. Report the slope either way.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds. The 1,260-segment pre-2022 calibration set exists and its detector scores exist; what is missing is DQI grades on it — roughly 1,260 gradings on the frozen rubric, i.e. an API-cost run, no new collection. Cheapest high-value test on this list.

gaps.gap: Single-family judge, with a measured style signal shared between the labelling screen and the grader (screen ai_guess vs grading-judge ai_guess r = +0.758), grading text partly produced by its own family in stage 6. Panickssery, Bowman & Feng (NeurIPS 2024) established self-recognition→self-preference as a measured mechanism with a linear dose-response, which makes 'the judge is Opus grading its own family's output' a named threat, not a hypothetical. The draft calls the cross-family replication 'the clean fix and owed' — a referee will simply ask for the owed thing.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Re-grade both main pools (1,522 segments) with at least two non-Anthropic judges — one frontier closed-weight (GPT-class) and one open-weight — on the frozen v2b rubric with the same anchors. Report per-dimension Spearman between judges, and re-run every claim-bearing cell under each judge, with the headline reported as a range across judges. Same for the stage-6 continuation arm, where the self-preference threat is sharpest.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds; API cost only, ~1,522 segments × 2 judges × 2 passes. No new collection.

gaps.gap: No prompt/codebook robustness reporting. Halterman & Keith (Political Analysis 34(2):188–204, 2026) document that LLM codebook classifiers are sensitive to element ordering, lean on label semantics rather than stipulated definitions, and fail on exclusion criteria — all of which bear directly on a seven-dimension rubric with in-context anchors and a conditional −1 code. S10 reports two passes at fixed prompt; that measures sampling noise, not instrument brittleness.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: On a 200-segment subset: (a) permute anchor order and dimension order across k≈5 prompt variants and report the between-variant sd of each dimension's mean plus whether the AI–human gap survives every variant; (b) an anchor ablation — grade with the Steenbergen anchors removed or scrambled — to demonstrate the anchors are load-bearing, which is the evidence the draft's own §8.3 validity argument assumes but does not show; (c) a definitions-only vs label-only ablation on one dimension to check the judge is using the DQI definition rather than the word 'justification'.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds; small API run, one afternoon of scripting.

gaps.gap: Unit-of-analysis mismatch with the instrument. DQI codes demand-bearing speech acts (Steenbergen: 56 speeches *that made a demand*; Gerber: 944 speech acts). S10 grades 'segments'. If AI-flagged segments carry a different number of demands per segment — which is plausible given they are longer and more monologic — then both the justification score and the headline applicability collapse (31.1% at screen ≥50) are partly segmentation artefacts rather than deliberative facts. The applicability finding is currently doing real work in §8.3, so this is not cosmetic.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Add a demand count to the rubric (and to gap 1's human coding), then re-express both applicability and justification per demand rather than per segment, and report demands per 100 words for AI-flagged vs human text. If demand density differs, report the applicability collapse as a demand-density result, which is a cleaner and more interesting statement anyway.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds; requires a rubric addendum and a re-grade of the two main pools (or a subsample), i.e. an API run.

gaps.gap: The equal-weight seven-dimension composite is asserted, not derived, and the draft says so ('the index's conventional additive form — rather than by any measured optimum'). The DQI literature does not treat this as free: Steenbergen 2003 justified index construction with a polychoric correlation matrix and dropped zero-variance components; Gerber 2018 used an item-response model; Behrendt 2024 derived weights from expert/non-expert correlations. Three of the seven dimensions are effectively null here, so an equal-weight composite dilutes the two real effects by construction.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Report the polychoric correlation matrix over the seven dimensions on the 1,522 graded segments and fit a one-factor graded-response IRT model; then re-run the AI–human contrast on the latent factor score. If unidimensionality fails, say so and retire the composite in favour of the per-dimension table (which is the stronger presentation regardless).
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds — pure re-analysis of committed id-keyed grades, no new grading, no API cost. Cheapest item on the list.

gaps.gap: 'No less engaged' is a null carried by three dimensions with MDE statements but no equivalence test. Stating an MDE is better practice than most published work, but it answers 'what could we have detected?' rather than 'have we ruled out a meaningful decline?' — and the claim in the abstract is the latter.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Two one-sided tests (TOST) on respect_demands, respect_counterargs and constructive in both stages, against a pre-specified smallest effect of interest (0.2 sd is defensible and should be registered before running), on the applicable-only subsample with speaker-clustered SEs. Report the equivalence CI per dimension. Do the same for the 63 within-text evasion pairs, where the null is currently the load-bearing reassurance in §8.3.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds; pure re-analysis, hours.

gaps.gap: No convergent validity against a second, independently-built instrument. Every quality number in the study comes from one LLM judge on one rubric. The Desai/Card/Jacobs survey finds convergent validity is the *most common* practice in published LLM-as-measurement work — S10 is currently below the median on the one dimension of validation the field actually does.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Score the same 1,522 segments with the AQuA adapters (open weights, github.com/mabehrendt/AQuA, multilingual BERT base, trained on 13,069 expert-coded comments and already validated on Europolis parliamentary-style speech) for justification, respect, storytelling and reciprocity. Report Spearman between AQuA scores and the judge's DQI codes per dimension, and whether the AI-flagged contrast reproduces on AQuA scores. Honest caveat to state: the adapters are German-trained, so an English transfer check is part of the deliverable rather than an assumption.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds; open weights, local GPU inference on 1,522 texts, no API cost, no new collection. A day's work including the transfer sanity check.

gaps.gap: No reference class for +0.29 sd. The number is uninterpretable without knowing what else moves this rubric by that much — a referee cannot tell whether machine drafting is a large effect on legislative deliberation or a rounding error next to being a minister.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: Report the same DQI contrasts for covariates already joined to the member panel: government vs opposition, front vs back bench, seniority/juniority, chamber, and prior-occupation altitude. Present the AI-flagged effect in a table beside them.
gaps.feasibility: Computable from data S10 already holds; the member covariates are already joined and the grades are id-keyed. Pure re-analysis.

gaps.gap: The whole quality arm is observational under an inferred treatment: 'AI-flagged' is a detector's guess, not an assignment. The two works that made this exact claim credible in their fields both had assigned provenance and human outcomes — Herbold et al. (Sci Rep 2023): 111 expert raters, 658 ratings, 2–3 raters per essay, Cronbach's α > 0.9, Holm-Bonferroni over 42 tests, Cohen's d 0.52–1.15; Kreps & Kriner (New Media & Society 26(12), 2024): 32,398 emails, provenance assigned, behavioural outcome. S10's stage-6 continuations are the right instinct — assigned provenance, matched content — but they are still graded by the same LLM judge, so they inherit gaps 1 and 4 rather than escaping them.
gaps.data_or_analysis_needed: A preregistered human rating study mirroring Herbold: recruit 50–100 raters with domain standing (legislative staffers, political-science graduate students), 2–3 ratings per text, length-matched machine/human pairs drawn from the actual corpus and from the stage-6 continuations, seven-dimension DQI rubric with the Steenbergen anchors in the instructions; report Krippendorff α or Cronbach α per dimension, Cohen's d, and multiple-comparison correction. This is also the strongest available answer to gaps 1, 3 and 4 simultaneously.
gaps.feasibility: Needs new collection — recruitment, ethics/consent, payment, and a rating platform. Weeks, not days, and the most expensive item here. It is the version of this arm that would survive review at a political-science venue on its own; the DSL route (gaps 1 + 2) is the cheaper path to the same referee-proofing and should be done first.

surveys.verdict: S10 exceeds the DQI literature on scale, transparency and adversarial self-criticism, and exceeds typical published LLM-as-measurement practice on robustness reporting — but it falls short on the one requirement both surveyed literatures treat as non-negotiable, a human gold standard the judge is validated against and the effect bias-corrected on, so the direction of the quality finding is well supported while the '+0.29 sd' figure is not yet referee-proof.

nearest_works.work: Krishna, Song, Karpinska, Wieting & Iyyer — "Paraphrasing evades detectors of AI-generated text, but retrieval is an effective defense" (DIPPER)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: A detector-agnostic paraphraser — never shown the target detector — defeats watermarking, DetectGPT, GPTZero and OpenAI's classifier; the same transfer setting as S10's threat model.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Five detectors spanning four families (watermark, zero-shot, commercial, supervised); three generator LLMs (GPT2-XL, OPT-13B, GPT-3.5-davinci-003); multiple domains (WikiText-103 open-ended, ELI5 long-form QA); every rate reported as detection accuracy at a FIXED 1% FPR (DetectGPT 70.3% → 4.6%); a deliberately capped attack budget — "we only paraphrase each generation once, rather than draw multiple samples until it evades detection"; semantic preservation quantified with P-SP against a human-paraphrase reference distribution (88–99% of paraphrases above the median human score) plus a human evaluation in Appendix C.2; a proposed defense (retrieval over 15M generations, 80–97% recovery at 1% FPR); models, code and data released.

nearest_works.work: Sadasivan, Kumar, Balasubramanian, Wang & Feizi — "Can AI-Generated Text be Reliably Detected?"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Recursive paraphrasing breaks every detector family, and reliable detection is impossible for a motivated adversary — the closest published analog to S10's "detection is not a security control" conclusion.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: Four detector families attacked (soft watermarking, OpenAI RoBERTa-Large, DetectGPT/zero-shot, retrieval); recursion depth reported as an explicit budget axis (pp1–pp5) with both single-pass and "best of" selection rates given separately; TPR@1%FPR reported throughout (watermark 99.8% → 9.7%, 4.0% best-of; RoBERTa 100% → 60%; DetectGPT AUROC 96.5% → 25.2%); text quality bounded three ways — perplexity (5.2 → 7.7–10.5), an MTurk human study (20 passages × 3 raters: 77% content preserved, 89% grammar acceptable), and a downstream-utility test (SQuAD-v2 QA accuracy retained at 97%); the reverse direction (spoofing human text into AI labels) measured as part of the same threat model; a theoretical AUROC/TV-distance bound tying the empirics to the impossibility claim.

nearest_works.work: Dugan, Hwang, Trhlík, Zhu, Ludan, Xu, Ippolito & Callison-Burch — "RAID: A Shared Benchmark for Robust Evaluation of Machine-Generated Text Detectors"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Detector accuracy claims of 99%+ do not survive adversarial conditions; the field needs a shared, attack-stratified protocol — this is the paper that set the current evaluation bar.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 12 detectors (8 open, 4 commercial: GPTZero, Originality, Winston, ZeroGPT); 6M+ generations over 11 generator models, 8 domains, 4 decoding strategies; 11 named attacks (alternative spelling, article deletion, homoglyph, insert paragraphs, number swap, paraphrase, misspelling, synonym, upper-lower, whitespace, zero-width space); a single primary metric — accuracy at a FIXED 5% FPR, justified by the cost of false positives; a full per-attack × per-detector table (Table 6) rather than pooled headlines (homoglyph −40.6 points averaged over five detectors; Binoculars −36.1 under synonym); public dataset and standing leaderboard so third parties can re-score.

nearest_works.work: Cheng, Sadasivan, Saberi, Saha & Feizi — "Adversarial Paraphrasing: A Universal Attack for Humanizing AI-Generated Text"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: A training-free attack that is universal and transferable: paraphrasing guided by one detector humanizes text against detectors it never saw.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 8 detectors across three families (4 neural: OpenAI-RoBERTa-Large/Base, MAGE, RADAR; 2 watermark: KGW, Unigram; 2 zero-shot: Fast-DetectGPT, GLTR); an explicit guiding-detector × target-detector transferability matrix (Fig. 4), i.e. the attack is scored on detectors outside the loop as well as inside it; relative T@1%F reductions reported per cell (64.49% RADAR, 98.96% Fast-DetectGPT, 84.94–87.88% average); a quality/attack-success tradeoff curve with three quality instruments (LLaMA-3.1-8B perplexity, GPT-4o Likert ratings of quality and semantic similarity, GPT-4o pairwise win rates); sampling parameters (top-p 0.99, top-k 50) stated as the attack's configuration; code released.

nearest_works.work: Masrour, Emi & Spero (Pangram Labs) — "DAMAGE: Detecting Adversarially Modified AI Generated Text"
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Commercial humanizers degrade existing detectors badly, and a data-augmented detector can be made robust to them — this is S10's own vendor, and the source lineage of the 2.31% humanizer baseline S10 divides into.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: 19 evasion products actually purchased and run (3 paraphrasers — DIPPER, Grammarly, QuillBot; 16 humanizers — Undetectable AI, StealthGPT, HIX Bypass, Phrasly, WriteHuman, Humbot, Twixify, Surfer SEO, etc.), i.e. the baseline is measured on the authors' own texts rather than cited from a vendor sheet; TPR at a fixed 5% FPR per detector before and after humanization (GPTZero 99.73% → 60.04%; Binoculars 94.15% → 28.23%); a three-tier manual quality taxonomy of humanizer output (L1 tone-preserving, L2 degraded, L3 nonsensical) with a GPT-4o fluency win-rate attached to each tier (26.0% / 14.67% / 2.67%); cross-humanizer generalization tested by holding tools out of training.

nearest_works.work: Perkins, Roe, Vu, Postma, Hickerson, McGaughran & Khuat — "Simple techniques to bypass GenAI text detectors: implications for inclusive education"
nearest_works.venue_year: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education 21:53 (2024)
nearest_works.what_they_claimed: Six commercial detectors fall from 39.5% to 17.4% accuracy under simple evasion, therefore detectors "cannot currently be recommended for determining whether violations of academic integrity have occurred" — the same institutional inference S10 draws.
nearest_works.evidence_they_marshalled: n = 805 machine-generated documents; six named commercial detectors run at their production operating points (the same setting S10 is in); a pre-specified inventory of evasion techniques applied uniformly so per-technique effectiveness is separable; unmodified-versus-modified accuracy reported as the headline contrast; false-positive rates for the same tools reported alongside (10–35%) so the policy conclusion rests on both error directions; data files deposited publicly (Mendeley xv6fk2mmh9). Companion standard-setter: Weber-Wulff et al., International Journal for Educational Integrity 19:26 (2023), 14 tools (incl. Turnitin, PlagiarismCheck) × human/AI/edited/translated/obfuscated document classes.

field_standard: Multiple target detectors spanning families — supervised/neural, zero-shot log-prob, watermark, and commercial API — 4 to 12 in accepted work; single-detector evasion results are treated as anecdotes about that vendor, not claims about detection.

An explicit transferability result: the attack must be scored against detectors that were not in the attack loop, ideally as a guiding-detector × target-detector grid (Cheng et al.'s central contribution; Krishna's whole design).

Rates reported at a stated fixed false-positive rate (1% Krishna/Sadasivan/Cheng, 5% RAID/DAMAGE), not at a vendor's default categorical label, so numbers are commensurable across papers and detectors.

Attack budget stated and held constant, with the single-pass rate separated from the best-of-N rate (Krishna caps at one paraphrase on purpose; Sadasivan reports pp1–pp5 and a separate 'best of' row).
Ground truth is known machine authorship of the seed text, not a detector's own prior verdict on it; the reported quantity is a true FNR on text the authors generated.
Semantic preservation of the attacked text measured with a similarity instrument (P-SP, embedding/NLI similarity) against a human-paraphrase reference distribution, not asserted.
